Senses.PreferredTarget: a hero in chaotic times
AlternateTargets: a hero of troubled times
Senses.Explanation: “A hero in chaotic times” characterizes drastic, forceful action as suited to disorder, usually in a pointed contrast with “a traitor in peaceful times.” Baichi Xingyuan and Yuan'an Liao apply the pair to blows and shouts versus refined talk. Baiyu Jingsi applies the hero half critically to Nanquan's killing of the cat. Lianfeng Su uses it for Yunmen's violent response to the newborn Buddha. Huiyue Xu turns the contrast into a warning at Bodhidharma's memorial.
Senses.Note: The expression is often ironic or double-edged, not simple praise. Its force comes from judging conduct against its conditions: what looks heroic amid disorder may itself be violent or out of place.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Yuanwu Keqin explains Xuedou's verse on Yunmen's bowl of rice and bucket of water. He rejects searching for a subtle theory underneath the plain answer, then warns that trying to understand without understanding and trying to stop without stopping only spills out a muddle-bag. He connects this hesitation with the verse's sons without trousers and quotes Hanshan afterward. Yuanwu voices the diagnosis to his audience; Yunmen and Xuedou supply the inherited material under examination.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1382.xml). In written instruction to monk Yue, Wuzhun Shifan compares learning with the moon waxing and then losing its light, beyond anything one can display to another. He recalls Guling returning to his teacher and claiming to be as he was before traveling. Yue now plans to visit his living teacher and father, so Wuzhun warns him first not to imitate Guling by spilling out a muddle-bag. He fears the teacher might act like Deshan and render even this written scroll waste paper. The phrase is Wuzhun's present warning against borrowed self-presentation, addressed to Yue.

Senses.Explanation: Spilling out a muddle-bag rebukes a confused attempt to present understanding. Yuanwu applies it to hesitation over Yunmen's answer, while Wuzhun warns a departing student against making a borrowed performance before his teacher. Neither passage recommends bewilderment as a way to teach. Yuanwu Keqin explains Xuedou's verse on Yunmen's bowl of rice and bucket of water. He rejects searching for a subtle theory underneath the plain answer, then warns that trying to understand without understanding and trying to stop without stopping only spills out a muddle-bag. He connects this hesitation with the verse's sons without trousers and quotes Hanshan afterward. Yuanwu voices the diagnosis to his audience; Yunmen and Xuedou supply the inherited material under examination. In written instruction to monk Yue, Wuzhun Shifan compares learning with the moon waxing and then losing its light, beyond anything one can display to another. He recalls Guling returning to his teacher and claiming to be as he was before traveling. Yue now plans to visit his living teacher and father, so Wuzhun warns him first not to imitate Guling by spilling out a muddle-bag. He fears the teacher might act like Deshan and render even this written scroll waste paper. The phrase is Wuzhun's present warning against borrowed self-presentation, addressed to Yue.

Senses.PreferredTarget: put a question
AlternateTargets: pose a question
bestow a question
Senses.Explanation: Literally, to let a question descend or to bestow a question. In Chan records it marks the bestowing master putting a question to monks and requiring an answer. The heading “questions put in the room” places it in the entering-interview setting; one such question asks how the patriarchal mind-seal is inscribed and how deep the buddhas' source is. An unnamed monk later recalls a question bestowed the previous day—“since it is not mind, not buddha, and not a thing, what is it after all?”—and returns to request instruction. Records also show questions put before a group: on a snowy day Pin Jixiang asks why the solitary peak is not white when snow covers the thousand mountains, and elsewhere monks give several replies to “when there is no buddha in the hall, what then?”, none of which Guxue Zhe accepts. The term therefore names an observable part of Chan's interview machinery: the bestowing master publicly or privately puts the question, monks answer or fail to answer, and the record preserves the ensuing acceptance, rejection, substitute response, shout, or blow.
Senses.Note: The literal downward/bestowing graph is retained in the alternate target, but ordinary English “put a question” best fits the repeated record headings and speaker turns. It is related to asking (問), public question-and-answer, answers supplied for others, and entering the room, but is not interchangeable with them.

Senses.Explanation: An indication is an address or showing offered to an assembly or interlocutor. The same referent appears as an act, a fixed case-preface rubric, and a catalogued textual item; these are grammatical and editorial packages, not different things. The compound occurs 721 times in 201 source files. The Blue Cliff Record's fixed rubric “the indication says” (垂示云) introduces Yuanwu Keqin's pointer before a case. One begins, “a phrase that settles heaven and earth, honored through ten thousand generations” (定乾坤句。萬世共遵。). Yunmen Wenyan's Extended Record counts “185 items of essential chamber sayings; 290 items of indications and substitute answers” (室中語要一百八十五則垂示代語二百九十則). Tianyin Yuanxiu's record prints “chamber indication” (室中垂示) before his words. Public interviews expose the same act from the requesting side: unnamed monks ask Jiufeng Qin and Shoushan Xingnian to offer an indication, while Touzi Datong asks Cuiwei Wuxue. The answers—including Cuiwei's ‘Do you want a second ladle of foul water?’—show Zen bending ordinary indication into a named teaching-seat event that can be requested, delivered, prefaced, and collected.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：水深多少？師曰：不乾。師因曹山辭，遂囑曰：吾在雲巖先師處親印寶鏡三昧，事窮的要，今付於汝。詞曰：如是之法，佛祖密付。汝今得之，宜善保護。銀盌盛雪，明月藏鷺。類之弗齊，混則知處。意不在言，來機亦赴。動成窠臼，差落顧佇。背觸俱非，如大火聚。但形文彩，即屬染污。夜半正明，天曉不露。為物作則，用󳫠諸苦。雖非有為，不是無語。如臨寶鏡，形影相覩。汝不是渠，渠正是汝。如世嬰兒，五相完具。不去不來，不起不住。婆婆和和，有句無句。終不得物，語未正故。重離六爻，偏正回互。疊而為三，變盡成五。如荎草味，如金剛杵。正中妙挾，敲唱雙舉。通宗通塗，挾帶挾路。錯然則吉，不可犯忤。天真而妙，不屬迷悟。因緣時節，寂然昭著。細入無間，大絕方所。毫忽之差，不應律呂。外寂中搖，繫駒伏鼠。先聖悲之，為法檀度。要合古轍，請觀前古。佛道垂成，十劫觀樹。如虎之缺，如馬之馵

Occurrences.Kwic: 總不如今日施主設齋供眾，一飽能忘百饑，老實求福要福、求壽要壽、求般若要般若。且道：般若還求得麼？者裏也須子細。不見龐公道：『難，難，十石油麻樹上攤。』龐婆道：『易，易，百草頭上祖師意。』靈照道：『也不難，也不易，饑來喫飯困來睡。』且問：還依那個即是？若是總依般若，豈有三路？若只依一路，爭奈公案不圓？若總不依，則莽莽蕩蕩。畢竟如何？還聽見方纔孩子聲麼？不見道：如世嬰兒，五相完具。」上堂，師召大眾，曰：「今日水月菴主為求干戈寢息，天下太平，要山僧陞座與他道取一句。山僧住持事繁，仰勞大眾代答一句看。」眾下語不契，遂下座，曰：「牛生三個子，到老自拖犁。」雲萍師請上堂。僧問：「雲師入山，為是因尋故舊？為復就裏呈機？」師曰：「一人傳虛，萬人傳實。」進曰：「賓主相見，所談何事？」師曰：「忙者不會，會者不忙。」進曰：「不落宮商曲，陽春和者稀。」

Occurrences.Kwic: 物作則之時，要用便用。若於餘時，無一塵繫念。涅槃經云：有所說者，名有為法。藥山却曰：第一不得絕却言語。他說箇語，是顯箇無語底也。如臨寶鏡，形影相覩。汝不是渠，渠正是汝。見道之者，如人臨鏡自炤，形影相對，不滯名言，寂然昭著。若纔以為汝，則汝外有渠，而汝不是渠，言汝者非也。若更以為渠，則渠全無渠，而渠即是汝，言渠者亦非也。是一涉名言，便成染污，豈妙契斯道之意哉？如世嬰兒，五相完具，不去不來，不起不住，婆婆和和，有句無句，終不得物，語未正故。涅槃經云：云何名嬰兒行？善男子！不能起、住、去、來、語言，是名嬰兒行。如來亦爾，不能起者，如來終不起諸法相；不能住者，如來不著一切諸法；不能來者，如來身行無有動搖；不能去者，如來已到大涅槃；不能語者，如來為諸眾生演說諸法，實無所說。經中舉嬰兒行以例如來之行，今舉以例法中具五位也。重離六爻，偏正回互
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian. Under the heading Commentary on Baojing Samadhi, Yongjue Yuanxian discusses the mirror image, quotes the infant line from Dongshan's poem, and then compares it with a sutra passage on infant conduct. Yongjue comments on the inherited verse; he does not become its original author.

Senses.Explanation: The line from Dongshan's Baojing Samadhi presents an infant as complete before learned speech or movement; later teachers cite it while discussing how direct realization appears. In the poem, the infant follows the mirror image of self and other, before lines about neither coming nor going and speech not yet settled. Shiyu Mingfang invokes the line while asking his assembly which inherited teaching to follow, pointing them to a child's first cry. Yongjue Yuanxian comments on the same verse after discussing the mirror image and then compares it with a sutra's account of infant conduct. These are one poem and distinct later uses, not separate original infant sayings.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Like someone climbing a mountain, each must make their own effort
AlternateTargets: As when climbing a mountain, each person must strive for themselves
SearchAliases: climbing a mountain each makes own effort
Senses.Note: A mountain cannot be climbed by another person on one’s behalf. Gaofeng uses the pair amid instructions for unbroken effort; Tianru follows a warning about death and delay with it. Shixi turns from an inherited case to his listeners’ responsibility, and Yuejiang uses it after describing the barriers they make of sensory experience. The image urges personal effort without claiming that teachers or companions are useless.

Occurrences.Kwic: 樞機，似一滴投於巨壑。到遮裏有甚麼禪道可參？有甚麼佛法可學？有甚麼生死可脫？有甚麼涅槃可證？騰騰任運，任運騰騰。臘月三十日到來，管取得大自在，去住自由。故云：自從認得曹溪路，了知生死不相干。然雖如是，豎拂子云：且道遮箇是生耶？是死耶？若也道得，便可向無佛處稱尊，無法處說法。其或未然，山僧不懼羞慚，更與諸人露箇消息。擲下拂子云：夜冷魚潛空下釣，不如收卷過殘年。兄弟家成，十年二十年撥草瞻風，不見佛性，往往皆謂被昏沈掉舉之所籠󰋪，殊不知只遮昏沈掉舉四字，當體即是佛性。堪嗟迷人不了，妄自執法為病，以病攻病，致使佛性愈求愈遠，轉急轉遲。設使一箇半箇回光返照，直下知非，廓然藥病兩忘，眼睛露出，洞明達磨單傳，徹見本來佛性。若據西峰點檢將來，猶是生死岸頭事；若曰向上一路，須知更在青山外。若論此事，正如逆水撑船，上得一篙，退去十篙，上得十篙，退去千篙，愈撑愈退，退之又退，直饒退到大洋海底，掇轉船頭，決欲又要向彼中撑上。若具遮般操志，即是到家消息。如人上山，各自努力。若論此事，如萬丈深潭中投一塊石相似，透頂透底，了無絲毫間隔。誠能如是用工，如是無間，一七日中若無倒斷，妙上座永墮阿鼻地獄。法門廣無邊，參禪第一義。若真師子兒，不入他羣隊。直下便翻身，諸獸皆迴避。毗盧頂上行，生死海中戲。佛祖不知名，眾魔爭敢邇。奇哉此妙門，寂寞無人思。若有發初心，須具大根器。內外絕諸緣，屏心立堅志。譬如人架屋，先須實基址。基實屋無傾，志堅道成易。提箇趙州無，截斷有無意。豎起鐵脊梁，急著眼睛覰。密密與緜緜，絲毫無間棄。譬如人倒懸，念念更無異。日夜苦思量，一心求脫離。不分東與西，寢食都忘記。又如初生兒，呼喚渾不視。用工到那時，如人鑽火燧。漸見黑黃烟，知火必在此。切莫顧危亡，更須加猛利。直待火星飛，通身是𦦨熾。余雖不會禪，也曾恁麼試。只在剎那間，可立而待至。頂門眼豁開，裂破娘生鼻。海竭須彌崩，虗空撲落地。十方賢聖師，盡是眼中刺。微笑與拈花，可煞不知愧。更有葛藤根，一千七百事。嗚呼後代人，盡食他殘饐。若更問如何，拳頭劈口捶。十二時中，四威儀內，寶劍全提，如臨大陣。纔有絲毫念起，當急剉之，一斷永斷，莫令再續。若能如是用工，管取干戈永息，天下太平。有志之士，思之遵之，夜後參前，遞相警勵。此事的要剋日成功，如善射者仰箭射空

Occurrences.Kwic: 事大，及參禪、念佛兩種法門而已。念佛者，只是靠取阿彌陀佛四字話頭，別無他說。若是初心參禪者，恐未有下手處、未有趣向處。然此亦無他說，只是汝諸人各各有箇本來面目，不曾認得這箇本來面目，直下與諸佛同體。你十二時中，語默動靜、行住坐臥，莫不承他恩力。但於此密密體認，即此便是下手處、即此便是趣向處也。便須直下承當，切忌等閑蹉過，發大勇猛、起大精進，要在箭鋒相拄、機筈相投。古人云：一不做，二不休，一拳拳倒黃鶴樓，一踢踢飜鸚鵡洲。有意氣時添意氣，不風流處也風流。果有古人如是作略，則德山與臨濟，與你是同參；釋迦與彌陀，阿曾有兩箇？併將千七百則諸祖機緣，與正法眼藏、涅槃妙心，穿作一串，颺在一邊，然後獨步大方，普告諸人道：丈夫自有通霄路，不向如來行處行。當此之時，則上座望風展拜有分。其或未然，莫恠壓良為賤，再下一箇註脚：世事茫茫沒了期，自家活計猛提撕。落湯螃蠏人人見，投火飛蛾箇箇知。病到始憐身是苦，死來惟有業相隨。浮光幻影須臾過，火急脩行也是遲。如人上山，各自努力。普達實立、副使．脫銕睦爾、副使．買奴海牙、同知．忙哥剌、宣差．馮總管等，率眾官士大夫來師子林設齋，請普說。師云：參禪是向上一著要緊大事。此事曰僧曰俗，人人有分，況是本來具足，全體現成。爭奈世間人往往當面蹉過，不曾去理會。莫道不曾理會，問也不曾問著。正眼看來，誠可憐憫。今日諸公既發此問，畢竟於此事上有大因緣。然此事纔擬說著，便是生死岸頭境界，便是痛心苦口之語。望諸公洗心滌慮，聽之思之。何謂參禪是向上要緊大事？蓋為要明心見性，了生脫死。生死未明，謂之大事。祖師道：參禪只為了生死，生死不了成徒勞。王右軍亦曰：死生亦大矣。豈不痛哉！只為生死事大，故以參禪為向上大事也。何謂生死？公等彼此有身在世，此身既不是諸佛如來金剛不壞之身，又不是純鋼打就、生銕鑄成底堅固之身，乃是四大假合、虗脆浮幻之身，如水上泡，如草頭露。看看髮白齒搖，皮枯面皺，老病無常，朝不保暮。既有生，必有死；既有死，還復生。但不知這回生死落在甚麼道中？此為可痛者也。佛說：三界如火宅，六道如苦輪。汝等從無量劫以至于今，向三界火宅中，東走西走，不知求出路；在六道苦輪裏，東輥西輥，無有暫停時。若欲息苦輪，出火宅，須是了生死；若欲了生死，須是見佛性；若欲見佛性，須是大悟一回；若欲

Occurrences.Kwic: 前句後鼓弄人家男女。何故？要且聲不是聲，色不是色，意在鉤頭。僧問：如何是聲不是聲？仁云：喚作色得麼？穿却鼻孔。如何是色不是色？仁云：喚作聲得麼？換却眼睛。僧禮拜。仁云：且道為你說，答你話，若檢點得出，許於佛法中有箇入處，分疎不下。後來雪竇云：本仁也是奇恠，要且貪觀天上，既非聲前色後，從什麼處入？應庵云：雪竇盡其神力，無插手處。只如道：既非聲前色後，從什麼處入？往往十箇有五雙蹉過。還知應庵落處麼？一箭落雙鵰。前輩恁麼互相提唱，不妨綿綿密密控你今人入路。兄弟既名參學，若不於此子細用心與古人相見，將來生死岸頭將何抵擬？山僧却有方便，不見僧問趙州：學人乍入藂林，乞師指示。州云：喫粥了也未？僧云：喫粥了也。州云：洗鉢盂去。僧於此有省。雲門云：且道趙州有指示無指示？若言有，趙州向伊道什麼？若言無，這僧為什麼便禮拜？真如󳭷禪師室中常舉此話，見學者擬下語，便以手掩其口云：歇去。且道真如意作麼生？徑山又不然，有下語者一任下語，只是不得動著。何故？如人上山，各自努力。法語法語示圓上人示圓上人見成公案，豈籍言詮？佇立寄私，垛生招箭。若夢遊區宇底，未免荏苒彷徨，拋家失業，驀忽惻然鼎省，翻得起來，却又不一頓刀刮水洗，心頭隱隱，似記似忘，敗闕愈甚。圓上人拖夢南來，欲求一句以助其省發，予便欲舉須彌槌擊虗空皷，又恐不能呼之。盖睡未稔，去去不能自已，於穿雲渡水時，平步失落，則眼子自開也。此時方可探南山虎穴，透鰻井龍門，先捏定他喉嚨，勿使轉側，方可拔其爪牙，戲其頭角。不尔，遭他一口，喪盡平生，雖曰善因，而招惡果。示源侍者示源侍者昔藥山訪道南嶽，始聞與麼不與麼㹅不得之語，如蚊子上鐵牛，逗到一物不為，閑坐則為；又似箇水上胡蘆子，按也按不住，只管皮膚脫盡，不知真實猶存，引得隨波逐浪。者道：我在藥山三十年，單明此事，種禾却生豆，試點檢他敗闕在什麼處？九上三到，桶底子打脫在木上座手裏，因何却向鰲山店上滯殻迷封？中夜聞豁公撾塗毒之音，返令鹽官色空義洞山過水偈動地放光，是曾郎久參事慢之過耶？西竺初祖呼二祖謂曰：倒却門前剎竿，著八字打開，兩手分付。何故？湧泉道：我四十年猶有走作。香林道：我四十年方打成一片。不出飛猿嶺，目貫九天；不下釣魚山，氣吞四海。備公回公，異代殊方，一狀領過十八上，破家散宅底，因甚老不休歇？無乃徒

Occurrences.Kwic: 水晶宮耳語箇什麼？擊拂子：一葉落，天下秋。小參小參□□□自然等編結制。無上法王有大陀羅尼門，圓而無內，方而無外，無內無外，聖凡普會。若入得此門，則百千三昧門、百千總持門、百千解脫門一時證入，二六時中、四威儀內撞倒燈籠、磕破露柱，且莫麤心好。睦州和尚道：未得箇入頭，須得箇入頭；若得箇入頭，不得孤負老僧。雪峯和尚道：盡大地是個解脫門，把手拽不入。且道古人意在什麼處？今時道流多是自生退屈、自生難易，未證謂證、未得謂得，聞聲被聲礙、見色被色礙、見空被空礙、見山被山礙、見水被水礙、見佛被佛礙、見魔被魔礙，欲得獨步大方，直須高超三界。何謂三界？貪是欲界、嗔是色界、癡是無色界。你一念貪便被水溺、你一念嗔便被火燒、你一念癡便被風飄，若離得者三種，便是出三界外。人聞聲不被聲礙、見色不被色礙、見空不被空礙、見山不被山礙、見水不被水礙、見佛不被佛礙、見魔不被魔礙、說長期短期不被長期短期礙、說安居禁足不被安居禁足礙，一切處自由、一切處無礙。拍禪牀，云：如人上山，各自努力。解夏。黃金真人鐵面具，開眼覰著，凜凜風生。遠山作眉紅杏腮，開得口來，早成話墮。東弗于逮打鼓，南瞻部洲小參。西瞿耶尼安居，北󳬂單越自恣。日月居忉利之上，四禪無風火之災。汝等諸人坐在清凉界中，那裏知得江南兩浙春寒秋熱。喝一喝。結夏。只此處便是妙峯孤頂，龍蛇混雜，凡聖同居。南來者上間安排，北來者下間安著。鼻孔廝拄，赤肉相挨。壁立萬仞底軟似綿團，和泥合水底渾鋼打就。耳裏著得無邊香水海，眼裏著得百億須彌盧。九十日內，佛眼也覰佗不破。只如大通智勝佛，十劫坐道場，因甚不得成佛道？待小溪水逆流，即向汝道。結夏清機，歷掌三十三天撲帝鐘；大用現前，當陽打動關南鼓。衲僧家舉一步，踏翻四大香水海，不喚作禁足得麼？動一念，推倒百億須彌盧，不喚作安居得麼？所以道：若立一塵，野老顰蹙；不立一塵，野老謳歌。百草頭上罷却干戈，閙市門頭識取自己。一月普現一切水，一切水月一月攝。成就八萬四千塵勞門，彈指三生六十劫。冬至。三世諸佛不知有，羊頭車子推明月。狸奴白牯却知有，沒底船兒載曉風。洞明格外真規，漏泄劫前消息。有句無句，如藤倚樹。樹倒藤枯，句歸何處。矮師叔三千里賣却布單即不問，老大溈因甚放下泥盤呵呵大咲。擊拂子。九九陽生第一爻，冬至寒食一百五。歲除，云：日遷月

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 樞機，似一滴投於巨壑。到遮裏有甚麼禪道可參？有甚麼佛法可學？有甚麼生死可脫？有甚麼涅槃可證？騰騰任運，任運騰騰。臘月三十日到來，管取得大自在，去住自由。故云：自從認得曹溪路，了知生死不相干。然雖如是，豎拂子云：且道遮箇是生耶？是死耶？若也道得，便可向無佛處稱尊，無法處說法。其或未然，山僧不懼羞慚，更與諸人露箇消息。擲下拂子云：夜冷魚潛空下釣，不如收卷過殘年。兄弟家成，十年二十年撥草瞻風，不見佛性，往往皆謂被昏沈掉舉之所籠󰋪，殊不知只遮昏沈掉舉四字，當體即是佛性。堪嗟迷人不了，妄自執法為病，以病攻病，致使佛性愈求愈遠，轉急轉遲。設使一箇半箇回光返照，直下知非，廓然藥病兩忘，眼睛露出，洞明達磨單傳，徹見本來佛性。若據西峰點檢將來，猶是生死岸頭事；若曰向上一路，須知更在青山外。若論此事，正如逆水撑船，上得一篙，退去十篙，上得十篙，退去千篙，愈撑愈退，退之又退，直饒退到大洋海底，掇轉船頭，決欲又要向彼中撑上。若具遮般操志，即是到家消息。如人上山，各自努力。若論此事，如萬丈深潭中投一塊石相似，透頂透底，了無絲毫間隔。誠能如是用工，如是無間，一七日中若無倒斷，妙上座永墮阿鼻地獄。法門廣無邊，參禪第一義。若真師子兒，不入他羣隊。直下便翻身，諸獸皆迴避。毗盧頂上行，生死海中戲。佛祖不知名，眾魔爭敢邇。奇哉此妙門，寂寞無人思。若有發初心，須具大根器。內外絕諸緣，屏心立堅志。譬如人架屋，先須實基址。基實屋無傾，志堅道成易。提箇趙州無，截斷有無意。豎起鐵脊梁，急著眼睛覰。密密與緜緜，絲毫無間棄。譬如人倒懸，念念更無異。日夜苦思量，一心求脫離。不分東與西，寢食都忘記。又如初生兒，呼喚渾不視。用工到那時，如人鑽火燧。漸見黑黃烟，知火必在此。切莫顧危亡，更須加猛利。直待火星飛，通身是𦦨熾。余雖不會禪，也曾恁麼試。只在剎那間，可立而待至。頂門眼豁開，裂破娘生鼻。海竭須彌崩，虗空撲落地。十方賢聖師，盡是眼中刺。微笑與拈花，可煞不知愧。更有葛藤根，一千七百事。嗚呼後代人，盡食他殘饐。若更問如何，拳頭劈口捶。十二時中，四威儀內，寶劍全提，如臨大陣。纔有絲毫念起，當急剉之，一斷永斷，莫令再續。若能如是用工，管取干戈永息，天下太平。有志之士，思之遵之，夜後參前，遞相警勵。此事的要剋日成功，如善射者仰箭射空
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1400.xml). Recorded sayings. Gaofeng urges sustained effort with the image of climbing a mountain, then promises a breakthrough from unwavering effort.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 事大，及參禪、念佛兩種法門而已。念佛者，只是靠取阿彌陀佛四字話頭，別無他說。若是初心參禪者，恐未有下手處、未有趣向處。然此亦無他說，只是汝諸人各各有箇本來面目，不曾認得這箇本來面目，直下與諸佛同體。你十二時中，語默動靜、行住坐臥，莫不承他恩力。但於此密密體認，即此便是下手處、即此便是趣向處也。便須直下承當，切忌等閑蹉過，發大勇猛、起大精進，要在箭鋒相拄、機筈相投。古人云：一不做，二不休，一拳拳倒黃鶴樓，一踢踢飜鸚鵡洲。有意氣時添意氣，不風流處也風流。果有古人如是作略，則德山與臨濟，與你是同參；釋迦與彌陀，阿曾有兩箇？併將千七百則諸祖機緣，與正法眼藏、涅槃妙心，穿作一串，颺在一邊，然後獨步大方，普告諸人道：丈夫自有通霄路，不向如來行處行。當此之時，則上座望風展拜有分。其或未然，莫恠壓良為賤，再下一箇註脚：世事茫茫沒了期，自家活計猛提撕。落湯螃蠏人人見，投火飛蛾箇箇知。病到始憐身是苦，死來惟有業相隨。浮光幻影須臾過，火急脩行也是遲。如人上山，各自努力。普達實立、副使．脫銕睦爾、副使．買奴海牙、同知．忙哥剌、宣差．馮總管等，率眾官士大夫來師子林設齋，請普說。師云：參禪是向上一著要緊大事。此事曰僧曰俗，人人有分，況是本來具足，全體現成。爭奈世間人往往當面蹉過，不曾去理會。莫道不曾理會，問也不曾問著。正眼看來，誠可憐憫。今日諸公既發此問，畢竟於此事上有大因緣。然此事纔擬說著，便是生死岸頭境界，便是痛心苦口之語。望諸公洗心滌慮，聽之思之。何謂參禪是向上要緊大事？蓋為要明心見性，了生脫死。生死未明，謂之大事。祖師道：參禪只為了生死，生死不了成徒勞。王右軍亦曰：死生亦大矣。豈不痛哉！只為生死事大，故以參禪為向上大事也。何謂生死？公等彼此有身在世，此身既不是諸佛如來金剛不壞之身，又不是純鋼打就、生銕鑄成底堅固之身，乃是四大假合、虗脆浮幻之身，如水上泡，如草頭露。看看髮白齒搖，皮枯面皺，老病無常，朝不保暮。既有生，必有死；既有死，還復生。但不知這回生死落在甚麼道中？此為可痛者也。佛說：三界如火宅，六道如苦輪。汝等從無量劫以至于今，向三界火宅中，東走西走，不知求出路；在六道苦輪裏，東輥西輥，無有暫停時。若欲息苦輪，出火宅，須是了生死；若欲了生死，須是見佛性；若欲見佛性，須是大悟一回；若欲
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1403.xml). Recorded sayings. Tianru closes a warning about impermanence and delayed effort with the pair.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 前句後鼓弄人家男女。何故？要且聲不是聲，色不是色，意在鉤頭。僧問：如何是聲不是聲？仁云：喚作色得麼？穿却鼻孔。如何是色不是色？仁云：喚作聲得麼？換却眼睛。僧禮拜。仁云：且道為你說，答你話，若檢點得出，許於佛法中有箇入處，分疎不下。後來雪竇云：本仁也是奇恠，要且貪觀天上，既非聲前色後，從什麼處入？應庵云：雪竇盡其神力，無插手處。只如道：既非聲前色後，從什麼處入？往往十箇有五雙蹉過。還知應庵落處麼？一箭落雙鵰。前輩恁麼互相提唱，不妨綿綿密密控你今人入路。兄弟既名參學，若不於此子細用心與古人相見，將來生死岸頭將何抵擬？山僧却有方便，不見僧問趙州：學人乍入藂林，乞師指示。州云：喫粥了也未？僧云：喫粥了也。州云：洗鉢盂去。僧於此有省。雲門云：且道趙州有指示無指示？若言有，趙州向伊道什麼？若言無，這僧為什麼便禮拜？真如󳭷禪師室中常舉此話，見學者擬下語，便以手掩其口云：歇去。且道真如意作麼生？徑山又不然，有下語者一任下語，只是不得動著。何故？如人上山，各自努力。法語法語示圓上人示圓上人見成公案，豈籍言詮？佇立寄私，垛生招箭。若夢遊區宇底，未免荏苒彷徨，拋家失業，驀忽惻然鼎省，翻得起來，却又不一頓刀刮水洗，心頭隱隱，似記似忘，敗闕愈甚。圓上人拖夢南來，欲求一句以助其省發，予便欲舉須彌槌擊虗空皷，又恐不能呼之。盖睡未稔，去去不能自已，於穿雲渡水時，平步失落，則眼子自開也。此時方可探南山虎穴，透鰻井龍門，先捏定他喉嚨，勿使轉側，方可拔其爪牙，戲其頭角。不尔，遭他一口，喪盡平生，雖曰善因，而招惡果。示源侍者示源侍者昔藥山訪道南嶽，始聞與麼不與麼㹅不得之語，如蚊子上鐵牛，逗到一物不為，閑坐則為；又似箇水上胡蘆子，按也按不住，只管皮膚脫盡，不知真實猶存，引得隨波逐浪。者道：我在藥山三十年，單明此事，種禾却生豆，試點檢他敗闕在什麼處？九上三到，桶底子打脫在木上座手裏，因何却向鰲山店上滯殻迷封？中夜聞豁公撾塗毒之音，返令鹽官色空義洞山過水偈動地放光，是曾郎久參事慢之過耶？西竺初祖呼二祖謂曰：倒却門前剎竿，著八字打開，兩手分付。何故？湧泉道：我四十年猶有走作。香林道：我四十年方打成一片。不出飛猿嶺，目貫九天；不下釣魚山，氣吞四海。備公回公，異代殊方，一狀領過十八上，破家散宅底，因甚老不休歇？無乃徒
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1405.xml). Recorded sayings. Shixi ends his own response to the Zhaozhou washing-bowl case by returning responsibility to each practitioner.

Senses.Explanation: Climbing the mountain is work each person must undertake. Gaofeng uses the line amid direct instructions for continuous effort. Tianru follows a warning about impermanence with the same injunction. Shixi concludes his response to a cited case with it; Yuejiang uses it after urging listeners past the barriers of sound and form.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Like someone reaching back for a pillow in the dark.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1382.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuzhun Shifan. Wuzhun applies the pillow image in a colophon after discussing use where use cannot reach, then addresses Yong’an.

Senses.Explanation: A bodily image for Avalokiteshvara’s hands and eyes changes speaker across old versions and gains two later uses. In J32, Yunyan asks Daowu what the many hands and eyes of Great Compassion do; Daowu answers with a person reaching behind for a pillow at night. The current teacher then adds his own verse on hands and eyes acting throughout the body. A J36 poetic retelling reverses the old exchange: Daowu asks, Yunyan gives the pillow answer, and the present author follows the dialogue with a new verse of candlelight and a moonlit scene. In a T48 live exchange a monk quotes the Daowu version and asks its meaning; the teacher replies that action can arise without a grasping mind and continues through the distinction between hands and eyes throughout and all over the body. Wuzhun Shifan applies the pillow image in a separate colophon to an axis associated with Yong’an, after speaking of use precisely where use cannot reach, and asks whether Yong’an accepts it. The source versions and later applications should be read in their own settings.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Like someone learning archery, only after long practice does one hit the target.
SearchAliases: learning archery long practice hits target
Senses.Note: The comparison concerns sustained examination and responsive use; no fixed timetable or mechanical guarantee is given.

Occurrences.Kwic: 保福拈問長慶：「嵒頭平生出世，有什摩言教過於德山，便道『猶較些子』？」長慶舉師示眾云：「若是得意底人，自解作活計。舉措悉皆索索底，時長恬恬底。觸物則傳，意在傳處。住則鏟住，去則鏟去。須於欲去不去、欲住不住處體會。不執物，不據物。不同窒塞人緊把著事不解傳得，恰似死人把玉擩玉相似。縱然傳得，直到驢年有什摩用處？且愧伊向這裏湊泊，不別運為。訝將去，鑽將去，研將去，直教透過，直教通徹。不見道『如人學射，久久方中』？」有人問：「中時如何？」師云：「莫不識痛痒摩？」保福云：「今日非唯舉話。」慶云：「是什摩心行？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (B/B25/B25n0144.xml). Zutang Ji (Anthology from the Patriarchs’ Hall). The Patriarchs' Hall anthology raises Baofu asking Changqing what Yantou could teach beyond Deshan's declaration that his school has no words or teaching to give. Changqing quotes Yantou's instruction to move freely without clinging to things or being obstructed by them, ending with learning archery and hitting the target only after long practice. Asked what happens when one hits, Yantou replies with recognizing pain and itching. Baofu then says the exchange is more than merely quoting a case. The exact pair belongs to Yantou's quoted instruction. Its patient practice is joined to responsive contact, not a guarantee that repetition of a fixed movement alone produces realization.

Occurrences.Kwic: 示濟禪人參禪人須參活句，莫參死句。何謂活句？只如僧問趙州：「狗子還有佛性也無？」州云：「無。」又問：「一切眾生皆有佛性，因甚狗子無佛性？」州云：「他有業識在。」這便是活句。這僧向活句上問，趙州又向活句上答。你如今要這一則公案分曉，只就業識紛飛處看。業識與麼紛飛，如何是無業識田地？佛性現成，如何得見佛性與佛祖一般？如人學射，久久方中，所謂得之於心，應之於手。卻不可滯在有上，滯在有上便同眾生；又不可滯在無上，教中謂之相違；又不可滯在非有非無上，教中謂之戲論。總不落階級，不涉廉纖，著著有出身之路，始到得活句邊，猶未取得老趙州性命在。且道老趙州性命作麼生取？不見五祖演和尚云：「趙州露刃劍，寒霜光焰焰，更擬問如何，分身作兩段。」你且道是死句？是活句？參。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB273.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Qianyan. Qianyan Yuanzhang instructs practitioner Ji to investigate living rather than dead sentences, raising Zhaozhou's refusal of Buddha-nature to a dog and the explanation of active conditioning. Look precisely where that conditioning flies about, he says: how is the ground without it and how can Buddha-nature be seen? He gives the archery pair and the relation between gaining something in the heart and answering through the hand. Yet one must not remain with existence, nonexistence, or neither, and even reaching a living sentence has not seized Zhaozhou's life. The headword is Qianyan's present comparison for sustained examination; its surrounding prohibitions prevent practice from becoming a fixed conceptual position.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1997.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. In a present instruction, Yuanwu Keqin says that being told to turn the light back can itself provoke another construction through seeing, hearing and knowing. To understand, one must let even traces of gain and loss or judgments fall away; he then revoices the archery comparison, where hitting comes after long practice. He raises Pei Xiu asking where the person in a portrait is, Huangbo calling him, his answering, and Huangbo's renewed 'where?' Yuanwu asks the assembly whether realization lay in the question or answer and warns against merely recognizing sounds and forms. The archery pair belongs to his current argument, rather than an explicitly attributed old Yantou quotation in this turn. It does not reduce the recognition in the following encounter to a measurable training timetable.

Entries.SourceTerm: 如人數他寶，自無半錢分

Senses.PreferredTarget: It is like counting another person’s treasure while having not half a coin oneself.
Senses.Note: The phrase belongs to the cited scripture or Buddha saying, not to the contemporary teachers as an original composition. The selected three settings are distinct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 看破一處，則千處萬處自然一一透過。」山僧說箇譬喻，此事如鳥抱卵，孜孜于動靜處不失所抱。抱來抱去，時節忽至、殼漏子七零八落，中間跳出箇活潑潑的來，便能知其饑飽、一動一靜，久久羽力皆全，又是一番無礙，南北縱橫，高低遠近，飛騰任意。確然之理，千經萬論也只與麼說，除此再無別事較量。不然縱通三藏窮盡五車，及餘諸子百家，若不死心故工夫，有箇悟門，總是外事。《華嚴經》云「如人數他寶，自無半錢分。」山僧也曾討經論、學機緣，到這裏都無用處。川老云：「欲知端的意，北斗面南觀。」透過，殼漏子七零八落；透不過，非但學者，任他川老也難分疏。山河石壁、草木叢林卻會此說，古今先聖盡被瞞了。若在此看往往埋沒，離此別說而又不然。天以之高，地以之厚；佛祖以之相續慧命，接物利生；山僧以之日用施為，逢場作戲；學者以之之乎也者，語言文字；百姓以之坐臥經行，著衣喫飯。于事于理
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB163.xml). Selected Record of Chan Master Guting’s Sayings. Guting Shanjian explicitly quotes the Huayan scripture’s treasure-counting warning while pressing students to practice directly rather than accumulate explanations.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Guting Shanjian explicitly introduces the line with 《華嚴經》云; the exact phrase is scripture, while Guting comments on learning without firsthand practice.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何面孔？此時如不諦當分曉，而無始習氣未得勦絕，於一切應緣處則不相應矣！學道人真如大火聚，一切大小名相俱不依倚，直教空蕩蕩，驀忽衝開頂𩕳隻眼，照破五蘊山頭，纔覺一生所習都成剩事。當此時節，佛眼覷不見，便恁麼承當得，真出窟獅子也。示泰徵汪文學示泰徵汪文學今昔士人博覽群書以資識性，而返記持古人言句納於胸中，當作事業、資談柄為極則，蓋以不知聖人闡教之意。吾佛有云：「如人數他寶，自無半錢分。」然聰明靈利人，易入而難保任，入處不深而力單弱。古德所謂靈利聰明人，纔聞善知識說著箇事，便眼目定動，早將心意識領解了也。似此非他咎，自作障礙，永無有悟底時節。既學此道，十二時中當淨意根下曠劫已來客塵煩惱、虛偽習染，單單提箇無義味話頭，如昔有僧問雲門和尚：「如何是佛？」門云：「乾屎橛。」蘊在胸中，遇物應緣處不得令絲毫走作、不容意地下卜度思量、不要別求解會。者
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB357.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiuyelin. In a letter to scholar Wang Taizheng, Xiuye Minglin cites the Buddha’s treasure-counting saying against collecting old words without doing the work himself.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Xiuye Minglin introduces the exact phrase with 吾佛有云 in his advice to Wang Taizheng; the named teacher cites rather than originates the verse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 德也。既發菩提心，當脩菩薩行。行若不脩，心成虗發。豈不見善財童子每參知識，必曰：我已先發阿耨多羅三藐三菩提心，而我未知云何學菩薩行、脩菩薩道。我聞聖者善能誘誨，願為我說。此乃善財發心脩行之樣子也。由是而知，雖有多聞，若不脩行，與不聞等。如人說食，終不能飽。故經云：如人說美饍，自餓而不食；於法不脩行，多聞亦如是。如人善方藥，自疾不能救；於法不脩行，多聞亦如是。如人數他寶，自無半錢分；於法不脩行，多聞亦如是。如聾奏音樂，悅彼不自聞；於法不脩行，多聞亦如是。如盲繪眾像，示彼不自見；於法不脩行，多聞亦如是。譬如海船師，而於海中死；於法不脩行，多聞亦如是。惟我某人則不然，一生所發都是菩提心，一生所脩都是菩薩行。妄想執著，念念遠離；智慧德相，時時體究。其於當來世中蒙佛授記、坐道場、成正覺，決定少他一分不得。且道有何憑據？擲主丈，下座。第七日，滿
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1403.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tianru Weize. Tianru Weize cites the treasure-counting line inside a longer scriptural verse on study without practice while teaching how bodhi mind must be enacted.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Tianru Weize says 故經云 before a longer verse on not practising what one has heard, including the exact treasure-counting line.

Senses.Explanation: Three teachers quote a scriptural warning that learning without practice leaves one personally empty. Guting Shanjian gives a long instruction on direct effort and explicitly quotes the Huayan scripture: someone who can count another person’s riches may still possess nothing. Xiuye Minglin writes to the lay scholar Wang Taizheng, says mere learning and collecting old sayings cannot settle the matter, and cites the same line as a saying of the Buddha before urging close work with a question. Tianru Weize cites it inside a longer scriptural verse comparing learning without practice to talking about food while going hungry; he is teaching bodhi mind and its enactment. The inherited scripture supplies the line, while each teacher addresses a different listener and practical failure.

SearchAliases: drinking water knows cold and warmth
Senses.Explanation: In these records, drinking water supplies a recurrent comparison for knowledge reported by the drinker: cold and warmth are known by the person who drinks. Literally, “like a person drinking water.” In the Chan record the phrase normally continues “knowing cold and warmth oneself.” Its Zen-specific use is as a stock comparison for knowledge that the person concerned reports from his own encounter rather than receives as another person's verbal description. In the Huineng and Huiming encounter, Huiming responds after Huineng's question about his face before his parents were born: “like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself.” Dahui says that at this point it is like drinking water and knowing its temperature oneself, and adds, “unless one has personally verified and personally understood, one can then see it.” The Record of the Mirror of the School frames a question with “understanding the way and clarifying the school are like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself—how can their manner be spoken?”, and elsewhere pairs the comparison with “only verification knows; it is difficult to measure.” Poshan states the same deviation in domestic language: “only each person understands inside his own belly”, followed by the water comparison. Thus the corpus retains the ordinary act of drinking but makes the drinker's private knowledge of cold or warmth its recurring Chan predicate.

Senses.PreferredTarget: As with drinking water, one knows its warmth or coldness oneself
AlternateTargets: Only the person who drinks the water knows whether it is warm or cold
SearchAliases: drinking water knows hot and cold
know for oneself like water temperature
Senses.Note: As a person who drinks water knows its warmth or coldness directly, so a student must discern the matter for himself. These masters use the older simile to test claimed understanding, direct a householder's inquiry, or urge care in everyday conditions. It does not mean that all responses are beyond discussion; the simile asks for personal verification.

Senses.Explanation: ‘As with drinking water, one knows its warmth or coldness oneself’ makes direct discernment as ordinary as feeling the temperature of a drink. Masters use it to press listeners beyond repeating an answer that belongs to someone else. Linquan applies the simile after questioning a verbal assessment of his case comment. Kongyin asks listeners to check themselves amid changing conditions rather than pretend to a settled state. Poshan says people share the same hall and senses, yet each must become clear for himself. Yingshan tells a householder to carry out his instruction until the matter is known without asking another person. Binya uses the line with cold and heat before a furnace address. Faxi writes that a teacher cannot pass this recognition by description and urges direct realization.

Entries.SourceTerm: 如今思量，當時不消道箇何必

Senses.PreferredTarget: Thinking back now, a 'why bother?' would have done back then.
SearchAliases: thinking back why bother would have done
Senses.Note: The qualified rendering follows the later comparison of why bother with no need; it does not certify Yunju's final standing or settle the rival replies into a universal rule.

Occurrences.Kwic: 示眾云：老僧二十年前住三峯庵時，有魏府興化長老來問，權借一問以為影草時如何？老僧當時機思遲鈍，道不得為伊，致得箇話頭奇特，不敢辜負伊。他云：想和尚答這話不得，不如禮拜了退。如今思量，當時不消道箇何必。後遣化主到魏府興化，化問：和尚住三峰庵時，老僧問伊話對不得，如今道得也未？主舉前話，化云：雲居二十年，只道得箇何必？興化即不然，爭如箇道不必？三聖云：雲居二十年，道得底猶較興化半月程。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp. Yunju Daoying tells the assembly that twenty years earlier Xinghua Cunjiang asked to borrow a question as a probe. Yunju could not answer, and Xinghua suggested he simply bow and withdraw. Thinking back, Yunju now proposes that a 'why bother?' would have done then. A later messenger carries this to Xinghua, who says Yunju has spent twenty years only arriving at 'why bother?' and offers 'no need' instead. Sansheng says Yunju is still half a month behind Xinghua. The headword is Yunju's retrospective proposed reply, with the elliptical wording rendered cautiously through the ensuing comparison. Neither the long interval nor the new reply receives an unqualified final confirmation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉：「興化問雲居：『權借一問以為影草時如何？』居無對。化云：『想和尚答此話不得，不如禮拜了退。』二十年後，居云：『如今思量，當時不消道箇何必。』後遣化主到興化處，化問：『和尚住三峰時，老僧問伊話對不得，如今道得也未？』僧舉前話，化云：『雲居二十年，秖道得箇何必。興化即不然，爭如道箇不必？』」師徵云：「古人一機未透，積歲窮研，豈肯造次，胡言亂道？今人不揣己分，纔入門來學些口頭三昧，便要為人師範，可不深愧古人乎？且道當時雲居道箇何必，興化道箇不必，還有優劣也無？試道看。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the same failed question, delayed proposal and Xinghua's alternative, then asks the present assembly to consider the ancients' persistence. They investigated an unpenetrated point for years, he says, rather than offering reckless talk. He contrasts this with beginners who learn a little ready-made mouth-talk and immediately want to teach others. Are Yunju's 'why bother?' and Xinghua's 'no need' better or worse? Tianyin asks for an answer. The exact retrospective phrase remains Yunju's quoted voice; Tianyin makes it a current test of sustained inquiry and claimed teaching ability. His praise of persistence does not decide the remaining comparison or establish the delayed wording as an approved response in every setting.

Entries.SourceTerm: 如今更思一頓，誰為下手

Senses.PreferredTarget: Now I would like another blow; who will deliver it?
AlternateTargets: I still want one more beating; who will lay a hand on me?
SearchAliases: Linji another blow who will deliver it
Senses.Note: The local challenge and the current teacher's response govern the reading; quoted evaluations are not universal factual claims.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟曰：「夫為法者不避喪身失命，我於黃檗先師處，三度問佛法的的大意，三度被打，如蒿枝拂相似，如今更思一頓，誰為下手？」時有僧出曰：「某甲下手。」師度與拄杖，僧擬接，師便打。憶得當年中毒來，懷抱何曾一打開，今日人前弄牙爪，擒龍捉虎活生埋。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. Linji Yixuan recalls asking Huangbo three times for the essential meaning of the Buddha's teaching and being struck three times, now likening the blows to a brushing with mugwort twigs. Saying that someone seeking the teaching does not avoid losing body and life, he asks who will give him another beating. A monk volunteers; Linji offers the staff but strikes as the monk reaches to take it. Feiyin Tongrong raises this case and answers in verse with poison received long ago, an unopened embrace, and the display of fangs and claws that captures dragons and tigers. Feiyin's forceful images appraise the old blows' continuing operation; the exact request remains Linji's quoted speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 臨濟遠祖云：「我二十年前在黃檗先師處三度問佛法的的大意，三度被打，如蒿枝拂相似，如今更思一頓，誰為下手？」時有僧出云：「某甲下手。」濟度與拄杖，僧擬接，濟便打。蓋其平生徹證超出過量，不與時輩合水和泥者比，比便是正脈、便是源流、便是耀古騰今大人境界也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. Baichi Xingyuan quotes Linji's recollection, the request for another beating, the volunteer and the blow delivered before he takes the staff. Baichi then explicitly praises Linji's lifetime of thorough verification as beyond ordinary measure, contrasting it with contemporaries who mix everything into mud. Senses.Explanation: Linji Yixuan recalls asking Huangbo three times for the essential meaning of the Buddha's teaching and being struck three times, now likening the blows to a brushing with mugwort twigs. Saying that someone seeking the teaching does not avoid losing body and life, he asks who will give him another beating. A monk volunteers; Linji offers the staff but strikes as the monk reaches to take it. Feiyin Tongrong raises this case and answers in verse with poison received long ago, an unopened embrace, and the display of fangs and claws that captures dragons and tigers. Feiyin's forceful images appraise the old blows' continuing operation; the exact request remains Linji's quoted speech. Baichi Xingyuan quotes Linji's recollection, the request for another beating, the volunteer and the blow delivered before he takes the staff. Senses.Explanation: Four questioners ask about the person within a place or scene and receive different replies. In Hanyu’s hall, a monk first asks about a lion’s realm. When he follows with the exact question about the person in that realm, the teacher answers with an image of upright dignity. In Defeng’s recorded teaching, a lay visitor asks about the local river crossing and then asks the same follow-up; the teacher responds by striking him. In Gulin’s setting, a monk asks about the Prajna realm and its person. The teacher answers with wooded hills and a stream, then describes eating barley gruel and resting on grass; a later question about eliminating both person and scene brings a blow. At Baishan, an unnamed questioner follows a question about the scene within a person with the exact question, and the teacher answers with an image of sky and a carried hat. The headword is a follow-up whose sense depends on the preceding realm question.

Senses.Explanation: The enthronement gauntlet that turns a new abbot's authority into a question demanding an instant display. Baiyu Jingsi, entering the abbot's quarters at Longhua where the old master ran his forge — bone-tapping, Buddha-smelting, nail-pulling — asks how this unworthy one will deploy, cracks his staff, and tells the hall to watch the command take effect; Guxue Zhenzhe, taking the room at Cuiyan where the ancestors pulled nails and loosened bonds for lake-and-sea monks, asks how Zhe deploys there and lets the seven-foot black rattan decide for you; Wanru Tongwei, taking the room at Caoshan, rules that Magadha's closed door and Vimalakirti's silence, though they cut off past and present, are unfit for the teaching, asks how this mountain monk deploys, and passes even the iron-browed copper heads only through the red furnace; and Jieweizhou Xingzhou, before the seat of the new Puji temple in the capital, asks how the new Puji will deploy, shouts once, and mounts the seat. Muchen Daomin, in the ceremonial-robe turn of his Tiantong enthronement, pictures shedding the jewels for hides and entering the market basket, asks how to deploy just then, and would overturn seas and ridges to find one who knows; Tianyin Yuanxiu, at the Yixing donors' xiaocan, grants heaven covers, earth generates, the king blesses, and ministers repay the state — then asks what the patch-robed one does with it, and the young Yulin, waiting at his side, overturns the incense table and cuts off the tongues of the world; Qiran Chaozhi, after quoting Dahui's bathing-the-buddha address, rules that for the supreme device the patch-robed monk's grip has not yet been dreamed of, then asks how after all to deploy — the cart is not pushed sideways, the truth not bent; and Lianfeng Su, having fallen as a young man into the old masters' pit and still unable to leap out with all his strength, asks the senior seat Langxuan how one deploys when one cannot get out, raising his whisk: flour is milled where the wheat grew, and songs must be sung in the emperor's home town.

Senses.Explanation: Three questioners and a fourth hall teacher ask for the One Vehicle in separate encounters. In Xuezui’s hall, a questioner cites the verse that only the One Vehicle is true and asks what that teaching is. Xuezui answers with cloud outlining mountains and water strengthening the sound of a stream. Yunmen Wenyan hears a different monk cite the teaching that the lands of the ten directions have only One Vehicle; Yunmen responds by asking why he does not ask something else, then shouts after the monk thanks him. Jue’an Kexiang quotes the claim that the lands of the ten directions have only one vehicle in his own hall. He asks the exact question and answers with plum-season rain, lotus fragrance, and a cool breeze before offering tea. In a separate hall preserved in the X68 collection, a monk asks the same question and the host replies with the top of a hundred-foot banner pointing to the sky. The same question thus meets a landscape image, a deflection and shout, a seasonal scene, and a banner-pole reply.

Senses.Explanation: The water question is one part of a sequence about a seal applied to sky, water, and mud. Four different teachers receive the question in otherwise separate exchanges. One answers with someone peering at a donkey through a well. Another says that the movement of past and present has no fixed stop. A third replies that a blue-eyed foreign monk could not put his mouth to it, and a fourth answers with a mud ox chewing cold ice in fire. The shared three-part sequence gives the question its frame, but each answer belongs to its own teacher and source scene.

Senses.Explanation: Four monks ask the same first question in three-seal exchanges and receive four different images. A J35 monk asks what one seal stamping emptiness means, followed by questions about stamping water and mud. The teacher answers the first with a bell at midnight; the other two receive a donkey and hoofbeats. In a second J35 hall a student asks the three questions, and the teacher answers the first that even the Buddha eye searching deeply sees no trace. In a third J35 conversation, the teacher replies to the first question with a wild goose whose flight leaves no clear east or west. A J37 monk asks the same sequence and receives a red sun above a high peak at the third watch, followed by moon and lamp images for the other seals. Each question is live in its own exchange; the repeated formula is a framework for different present replies.

Senses.Explanation: A monk asks how to recognize the third of Linji’s four shouts, the one compared with a probe pole and watching movement in the grass. The exact clause is a question about one particular function of a shout in the Linji set, distinct from a generic shout. In Xiangya Ting’s hall a monk asks all four kinds; Xiangya lifts his whisk and asks whether he understands the probe-grass kind. Jiguan Huo answers the same third question by telling the monk that he now knows him, then strikes when the monk asks for a still more direct disclosure. Zhe’an Jingfan answers by invoking a mirror held in the hand that cannot hide beauty or ugliness. In another liberation-day hall Shending Yikui answers by asking whether the monk feels pain or itch. Each teacher uses the inherited fourfold frame for a present exchange, with a different diagnostic move at this exact third question.

Senses.Explanation: A monk asks about the sword-like function of the first of Linji’s four shouts, and four teachers demonstrate it with different verbal or physical responses. The exact clause singles out the diamond-king sword shout within Linji’s fourfold teaching, rather than asking about a shout generally. Feiyin Tongrong receives all four questions from a monk and answers this one by saying the person has already been cut into two parts. In Tian’an Sheng’s hall a monk first asks leave to inquire into the four shouts, then asks the sword question; Sheng shouts and drives the monk back with repeated blows when he tries to continue. Faxi Yin receives the four questions during an invited hall address; he strikes at the sword question and says its light appears before the blade leaves its sheath. Jie’an Jin hears a monk frame the question with peace among six states; he replies that the monk does not know its danger, then continues the other shouts. These are four separate live scenes with the same precise subtype and different responses.

Senses.Explanation: A question from the Jiufeng and Shishuang case is put to teachers in three distinct settings. At a J29 New Year eve talk, a monk moves through questions about the end of the year and the origin of things, then asks what it means to go as one strip of white silk. He says the senior monk had sat down on the single-color side, then imagines asking him the white-silk question and answering with cold light shining across the earth. In a J39 exchange, a monk asks Xingkong Zhen the same question and receives a terse call to look underfoot. The monk then quotes Jiufeng and continues to press the teacher. Senses.Explanation: An inherited question about one color receives separate critique, a fresh answer, and a proposed replacement. Tianyin quotes a monk asking Guanxi what one color is. Guanxi answers that it does not follow, and Tianyin challenges his own audience to recognize the old reply rather than merely settle at one-color language. In Rujiu Ruibai’s hall, a monk asks the same question as part of eight doctrinal questions. The teacher answers with an old peak sealed by cloud and follows it with a verse about color, mind, and perception. Shending Yikui quotes an older question to Zhiyuan, then poses it again hypothetically and says his own reply would be that dragons and snakes, ordinary people and sages, mingle together. In Wanru’s hall a monk says ancient and present are one color and asks what that color is; Wanru replies that there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions. The four scenes use a common question to test whether unity has become a fixed idea.

Senses.Explanation: The question presses a student or novice to show what resolve means in action. Feiyin asks the temple officer Guyuan what the task of such a person is after Guyuan says that he and the teacher are both men of resolve. Guyuan answers with a claim of singular honor, and Feiyin presses him further. Tian’an Sheng raises the question during a novice’s head-shaving ceremony after saying that a person of resolve must form and carry out a corresponding intention; his response evokes a blade that cuts decisively. In Jifei’s release-of-retreat tea gathering, the teacher asks a monk this after rejecting the monk’s answer about passing the examination with an empty mind. The monk requests the teacher’s confirmation, and Jifei presses him again. The phrase tests conduct beyond an easy declaration.

Senses.Explanation: An old three-part going-and-coming exchange is challenged in two later halls, alongside two separate present questions. In J32 an unnamed monk asks who neither comes nor goes, after asking about departure and return; the teacher replies with a stone woman calling the three realms awake and a wooden man stopping the six sense gates. In J39 a lay visitor reaches the same third question, the teacher shouts, the visitor shouts back, and the teacher strikes before drawing him along. Songyuan’s X70 comment quotes Tong’an’s older three-question sequence and faults its way of handling the matter. Gulin Qingmao in X71 raises Tong’an and Songyuan again, judges both insufficient, and proposes further counter-responses in his own hall. The repeated question has distinct live speakers and two separate critical uses.

Senses.Explanation: A monk puts the same technical question to three different teachers, who answer with different images. In Ruibai Mingxue’s teaching on stages of borrowing, an unnamed monk asks in turn about borrowing, borrowing again, and borrowing without borrowing. Ruibai answers the exact question with a stone ox giving off warmth in winter, then adds a verse about walking alone by moonlight. In Liangting’s hall, a monk cites earlier sayings about borrowing and presses through the same sequence. Liangting answers the exact question with the phrase “returning along the way and obtaining the subtle,” then handles a further question about completely surpassing borrowing. In Wenmu Nian’s hall, another monk asks the exact question during a series about function and rank. Wenmu responds with a cold pool at midnight and an ape calling in a high tree. The shared question is part of a technical dialogue; the distinct answers anchor each occurrence to its own exchange.

Senses.Explanation: An old monk asks Muzhou for a word beyond elaboration; later teachers challenge that answer and offer contrasting replies of their own. Muzhou Daoming’s old exchange pairs a question about an elaborated saying with the question about a saying not unfolded in explanation; Muzhou answers the latter with a ritual farewell formula. Dahui Zonggao cites that case, praises Muzhou’s responsiveness but says the answer reaches only eight tenths, and gives a shout in his own proposed reply. Fangrong Ruxi quotes Muzhou and Dahui, finds Dahui too showy, and supplies another answer while inviting the assembly to examine the chain of criticisms. Yunwai Xingze likewise quotes the old case and Dahui, says both teachers bite only the red side of a plum, and provides a fresh answer for his own hall. In a direct Baoen record, Yulin Tongxiu critiques Dahui as adding mud to earth and imagines someone asking Baoen the same question; he answers with a voice like thunder. The old quoted monk voices the clause in the first three chosen passages; Yulin stages a hypothetical visitor in the fourth. These are distinct present appraisals of one inherited problem, not four separate original Muzhou encounters.

The teacher answers the middle question by saying “recite a thousand, recite ten thousand,” then raises a bamboo strip for the last. At a J38 memorial service, the question about the middle form receives a second blow, after a first blow for the empty form; the teacher uses his staff for the third. Another J38 teacher answers the not-empty form with the Yellow River under a lid and contrasts it with an empty form represented by a bottomless bowl. In X68, a monk asks the same sequence and the teacher answers the middle question with waking up and eating, between sleeping after a meal and eating by day and sleeping by night. The questions repeat, while the answers differ sharply.

Senses.Explanation: Shushan Kuangren asks Guishan for a response outside sound and form, then challenges the whisk gesture he receives; later teachers dispute what either man understood. In Guishan Lingyou’s recorded saying, Shushan Kuangren hears Guishan urge travellers to move freely among sound and form and asks what a line outside them would be. Guishan raises a whisk; Shushan judges that gesture to have fallen into sound and form and departs. Miaoyun Zhenxiong later quotes the encounter and argues that Guishan showed the root while Shushan missed it; Miaoyun imagines a sharper intervention of his own. Xutang Zhiyu recounts the encounter in a much longer instruction, explaining Guishan’s silent gesture and why Shushan found a later answer from Xiangyan insufficient. The anthology preserves named later appraisals as well: Longxiang Xin reverses the usual judgment, saying Guishan lost an eye and Shushan saw through him, and Zhongfeng asks listeners whether they accept that verdict. The three direct records carry the original case and two distinct authored readings; the anthology is retained only for that separately named later challenge, not as another original dialogue.

Senses.Explanation: An inherited question about non-migration receives later criticism and two separate present replies. A monk in Tongtian Yisou Gao’s hall asks first about the meaning of moving and hears that the sun rises in the east while the moon sinks in the west. He then asks the exact non-migration question; the teacher says that the monk’s eyes have already been changed. The X67 case collection records an older monk asking Jiufeng the same question. Jiufeng answers with stars circling the north at night and flowers covering the courtyard steps. Later commentators in that source test both the answer and the monk’s failure to grasp it. Liaotang Weiyi in X71 cites a different old exchange: a monk asks Baishui Benren the exact question and hears of falling flowers, flowing water, and a moon above a peak. Liaotang then says Baishui has spoken only eight tenths of it and offers his own colorful counter-answer. In a separate present hall, a monk asks Yu’an Zhiji the question and hears that the sun comes from the east and sets in the west at night. The four deployments keep the older Jiufeng and Baishui questioners separate from the present monks.

Senses.Explanation: A monk asks how the Buddha can have a saying without speaking; four teachers answer the question in their own present dialogues. The question pairs the Buddha’s unspoken saying with Mahakasyapa’s hearing without hearing. At a hall address requested by a layman, a monk asks Shiqi Tongyun the first question; Shiqi asks whether the monk is deaf, then strikes when the exchange continues. At a Buddha-enlightenment-day address, Lianyue Daozheng answers that the tongue does not leave the mouth and follows with an account of awakening and teaching. Yunwai Xingze responds with the sound of clear chimes beyond right and wrong, then gives a separate answer about Mahakasyapa. In Buyan Le’s brush-holding session, the teacher says the voice is like thunder and makes a listening gesture when the monk asks where Buddha and Mahakasyapa are now. The full question functions as a test of saying and hearing rather than a claim that the Buddha directly spoke these words.

Senses.Explanation: A monk reaches the fourth part of a four-realm sequence and asks how phenomena can be unobstructed among one another; teachers answer with actions and vivid local images. In the northern travels record a monk asks Muchen Daomin in turn about principle, phenomena, their mutual nonobstruction, and the realm in which phenomena do not obstruct phenomena. Daomin raises his whisk and puts it down, saying he has discussed it intimately. Yuan’an Liao receives a similar four-question sequence in a hall address and answers the fourth with a startling image of a dog at the Buddha hall steps. Jifei Ruyi answers a current monk’s fourth question by saying that demon palaces and tiger dens are all places of practice. In Yuanwu Keqin’s memorial small gathering an unnamed monk asks the same sequence; Yuanwu answers the fourth with inexhaustible layers and the real body appearing everywhere, then expands the point in his own address. The exact question is the monk’s utterance in each scene; each teacher’s answer provides a separate source-local use of the inherited fourfold frame.

In a Yezhu hall, a different monk asks the sequence and hears of a fire in the night burning out an old person’s grave. Shenfeng Xian answers another monk with cloud over the southern mountain and rain over the northern one. In the Yuan’an Feng record, a monk asks the same band and hears that the whole array of appearances makes it plain. Yuan’an continues with replies for the other bands, including a millstone moving through empty space. The phrase names one place in a known series, but the images and teaching exchanges are local.

Senses.Explanation: Four monks ask the last question in a setting-person-meaning sequence; the teachers answer with silence, blows, and a challenge. At Tianyin’s hall, a monk asks first about the setting and then the person within it. When he asks for the meaning within the person, Tianyin lowers his whisk and remains silent for a while. Wufeng’s monk asks the same three-part sequence and receives a blow at the last question. At a hall requested by lay supporters, Feiyin’s monk asks about Huangbo’s setting and its person. Feiyin tells him to recognize the answer himself when he asks for the meaning within the person. In Shiqi’s hall, a fourth monk asks about Xuedou’s setting and its person; Shiqi strikes him for the final question and continues the sermon. The question’s place in the sequence is shared, but the named settings and answers are local.

Senses.Explanation: What is it when both person and environment are taken away? (如何是人境兩俱奪) is the question form of the third member in a recurrent four-part sequence: the person taken away but not the environment, the environment taken away but not the person, both taken away, and neither taken away. The records do not supply one stock answer. Linji Yixuan answers with ‘news cut off from Bing and Fen, dwelling alone in one region’; Yinyuan Longqi puts down his staff; Tianyin Yuanxiu tells the questioner to stand aside and, in another recorded exchange, says that there is neither one who explains the teaching nor one who listens. The retained lamp recension records Sanjiao Zhisong answering, ‘a headless toad points a foot at the sky.’ The stable lexical unit is the question and its place in the four-part sequence, not any one response.

Senses.Explanation: A traditional bridge question receives four different local answers. At a birthday sermon an unnamed questioner asks about a person crossing a bridge; the teacher tells him to watch his footing. In a second exchange a layman asks and the teacher rejects the premise, saying there is no water and asking what bridge he means. A third monk hears the teacher ask what it is. In the fourth hall a monk receives an image of ten people sinking, nine and a half of them gone. The same inherited series about an empty hand, an ox, and a bridge receives different present responses.

Senses.Explanation: The stock public-interview demand for the central point of the buddhas' teaching. Daolin answers Bai Juyi with 'do no evils; carry out the many goods'; Qingyuan Xingsi asks an unnamed monk the price of rice in Luling; Linji Yixuan shouts at one unnamed monk and raises the whisk before striking another; Zhaozhou Congshen tells an unnamed monk to pay his respects and then cuts off the attempted continuation. When Ding Shangzuo asks, Linji leaves the Chan seat, seizes Ding, slaps him, and pushes him away. Xuedou Chongxian answers another unnamed monk with 'five-colored auspicious clouds.' The repeated formula is one public demand, while its recorded replies range across maxim, counter-question, shout, implement, image, and bodily action. The records supply no single answer shared by all these exchanges.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask about the highest vehicle and receive concrete answers instead of a doctrinal definition. A monk asks Wuhuan about the time before Bodhidharma arrival and afterward, then asks what the highest single vehicle is. Wuhuan answers with vines passing through and binding split bamboo, and gives another short reply when asked for the meaning. In a J33 exchange, a monk puts the same question to Zizhou and hears that the food lacks neither salt nor sauce. When he bows, the teacher presses him to say what flavor he has tasted and strikes him. A J38 teacher answers a third monk with a golden hook floating on water, then moves into other questions about speech outside the usual frame. The three local exchanges keep the question while changing its teaching image.

Senses.Explanation: The first-step question is asked by a monk, a teacher testing an attendant, an official, and a hall host. A J28 monk quotes the saying that a thousand-mile journey begins with one step and asks what that first step is. The teacher stamps his foot and asks whether the monk understands, then answers later questions with his staff. In J33 a teacher puts the same saying to Jing Weina, who answers by telling him to look under his feet; the teacher threatens blows, and the attendant replies that even these are unnecessary. In a J34 tea conversation, official Huang asks how to take the first step while far from home. The teacher answers with wind stirring flowers, then follows the official through questions about the road and the inner chamber. At a J37 monastery opening, the teacher asks the first-step question himself before ascending the seat. He strikes his staff and answers that one should look beneath the feet. The same short question shifts from request to challenge according to who speaks it.

Senses.Explanation: Four separate questioners ask for the first sentence and hear a feeding image, a backward step, an invitation, or another question. In Sanyi Yu’s record, the first-sentence question receives the image of chewing rice to feed a baby. A verse after the answer probes the use of such teaching. A lay visitor in Xueguan’s hall asks the same words after questions about several Buddha bodies. Xueguan tells him to step backward and recognize it; the subsequent final and middle sentences receive other replies. At Yunfu Zhi’s hall, another monk asks for the first sentence and is told to come forward. The monk asks for the final sentence, and Yunfu says it has already been spoken. In Huigong’s hall, a further monk asks after a different barrier exchange. Huigong counters by asking what there was before the monk asked at all, then continues to answer requests for other sentences. The fixed phrase marks a starting point; each teacher makes the listener act or reconsider it.

Senses.Explanation: A numerical Chan riddle is used in three separate exchanges, including one where the teacher asks it. In a Guxue exchange, the teacher questions a monk about the dharma body, what lies beyond it, and why a clear matter is not heard. Guxue then asks what the former three and three are; the monk answers with a seamless round object and answers the matching latter question with a line about wind. Guxue warns him not to become tangled in vines when chopping firewood. In a separate Miyin teaching, a monk asks the former three and three question and receives an image of a lantern riding a horse out of the mountain; the corresponding latter question receives a pillar riding an ox over water. In Yunshan Yan Jushen record, a monk asks about both former and latter three and three in one breath. The teacher replies by repeating the pair, then cries out to the sky when the monk asks how many that makes. The three exchanges keep the numerical riddle open through different answers and speaker roles.

Senses.Explanation: Four separate questioners ask about the transformation body in teachings on the three bodies. In Rujiu Ruibai’s tea conversation, a lay visitor asks in turn about the dharma body, the reward body, and the transformation body. The teacher answers the last question with the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. At Zhaojue, an unnamed questioner follows two questions about the bodies with the exact third question, and Xuezui replies with an image of people circling Shizhi Mountain. Sanshan Lai answers the three questions in a staff demonstration: he turns the staff over, raises it, then answers the transformation-body question with a playful account of the staff disturbing Shakyamuni and returning to his room. Hanxiu answers another monk’s series with the Yellow River flowing east. The shared wording names a doctrinal body, while each local exchange gives it a different concrete response.

Senses.Explanation: Four questioners invoke the ten wisdoms, and the responses range from a rebuke to a detailed list. A J39 assembly leader asks about the ten wisdoms after the teacher has struck him and told him that was yesterday answer. The teacher treats the new question as idle equipment, then answers each follow-up in a long series of images. A J40 teacher first quotes Fenyang list and challenges the assembly to identify its ten parts. A monk asks the exact headword, and the teacher launches a fresh, deliberately startling set of answers. In an X68 exchange, a monk asks a lay ruler the question. The ruler replies with a descending list from nine bands to a single sentence, and their dialogue continues over what the monk calls entangling words. In an X70 encounter, a questioner recalls Fenyang teaching on the ten wisdoms, asks the exact question, and receives “carrying water and setting a fire” before asking each of the ten parts. Each local exchange tests whether a received scheme can be handled in speech.

Senses.Explanation: An emperor's question to a national teacher and a monk's variant to Touzi receive separate later readings. Emperor Suzong asks Nanyang Huizhong what the ten-bodied Tamer is. One version has the national teacher stand and ask whether the emperor understands; another transmits a different verbal reply. In a J27 appraisal the current writer asks what the national teacher's act of standing accomplishes. A J34 poet sets the imperial question before a verse warning readers not to stare at the water vessel alone. A J35 poet takes a variant of the imperial dialogue and answers with a distinct verse challenging easy identifications of the pure Dharma body. Another J35 author instead cites an unnamed monk who asks Touzi Datong the same question; Touzi simply rises from his seat, and the later teacher tests how to distinguish two similar gestures. A J39 hall teacher asks the assembly what Huizhong's standing accomplished; a J38 Lei-feng teacher adds a verse on Touzi's rising. The imperial and Touzi questioners remain distinct.

Senses.Explanation: A lay visitor asks a teacher where Chan study becomes effective, within a short sequence about its difficulty and use. Tang Qiyuan visits Rujiu Ruibai in his room and asks where Chan study gains strength. Ruibai says that it is settled at every point; Tang then asks where study is difficult and where it can be used, receiving separate answers. In Shiyu’s record an unnamed lay visitor asks the same three questions. Shiyu answers the strength question with boundless spring at the tip of his fly whisk, then warns the visitor not to linger over streams and mountains when asked about difficulty. Tang later asks Xueguan the same strength question after asking where to begin and where the danger lies. Xueguan replies with grasping heaven and earth; a following monk asks the same sequence and receives a different reply about a boat opening against the current. The two Xueguan records preserve the same encounter, so only one is retained. The question asks for the operative point of studying Chan, and each teacher answers inside an encounter rather than giving a general study method.

Senses.Explanation: Four monks ask the ruler-and-minister question and receive four different images. In Hongjue Min’s northern tour, a monk asks a full sequence of ruler and minister questions. For how the ruler regards the minister, Min answers that heaven covers him and earth accommodates him. In Ruibai’s record, a separate monk asks the same place in the sequence, and Ruibai answers with a clear mirror reflecting a flower grove. At Boshan Wuyi’s hall, another monk receives an image of an old mirror hung with white silk, then continues to ask how the minister turns toward the ruler. In Guxue’s hall, a monk asks after a question about the five ranks and hears of the bright moon reflected in a wave’s heart. The fixed question locates one relation in the five ranks while the teachers answer with their own metaphors.

Senses.Explanation: Four monks ask the same three-bodies sequence and receive different concrete replies. In a J27 hall a monk asks successively about the pure Dharma body, the complete reward body, and the many transformation bodies. The teacher answers the middle question by asking whether the monk wants another ladle, and strikes after the last question. In J28 another monk asks the sequence; the teacher answers the reward-body question with six faculties fully present, then insists that the point must be indicated directly. A J29 teacher answers with Guanyin Tower, placing a local landmark where an abstract category might be expected. In J38 a monk asks the three questions and the teacher uses his whisk differently for each: held upright, pressed sideways for the complete reward body, and waved for the transformation bodies. When asked which body teaches, he strikes the whisk three times. The recurring formula is tested through four independent exchanges rather than one inherited answer.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask about the local Bao’en setting and receive different place-based answers. At Tianyin Yuanxiu’s Bao’en hall, a monk asks for the scene of Bao’en after a question about its characteristic sentence. Tianyin answers with clouds over Ladder Ridge and water running below Golden Cart Mountain, then responds to further questions about a person and that person’s meaning with his whisk. At Huayan Shengke’s new Bao’en installation, another monk asks the exact question after the opening incense and ritual. Huayan answers with an iron pole on Zhenwu Mountain and follows with answers about the person of Bao’en and a sentence for the occasion. In the Lianfeng record, a monk asks the same question during a hall requested by several patrons. The teacher describes a mountain rising behind the hall and a bridge holding the water before its gate. The three answers point to distinct local scenes rather than one fixed doctrinal definition.

Senses.Explanation: A written answer and two present interviews distinguish outward succession from inward inheritance. In a written sequence on inner and outer succession, Sanshan Lai gives an outward-succession question and answers with images of travel and service amid worldly dust. At Zhufeng’s hall, a monk asks the same question after asking about inner succession. The teacher replies with military and court images of taking command and aiding the realm. In Yongjue Yuanxian’s discussion, a questioner cites an older distinction between outward succession as the minister’s position and inward succession as the royal line. Yongjue confirms it, then explains that outward succession has yet to know the inward matter fully. The question tests how a teaching passes into action without treating a visible role as the whole inheritance.

Senses.Explanation: Duofu’s old bamboo question becomes an awakening story and prompts separate later verses and alternatives. In the old exchange a monk asks about Duofu’s clump of bamboo, and Duofu answers with slanting stems, then curved stems when the monk does not understand. A later teacher tells how reading that exchange awakened a seeker and asks his own assembly what the great matter is. Two other teachers place the old question before their own different verses, one using clouds and clear wind and the other offering a pine tree at a thousand cliffs. A fourth teacher quotes the old case, substitutes a new question about Juyun’s bamboo, and supplies his own answer and verse. The older dialogue is one family; the later deployments differ.

Senses.Explanation: A traditional question is asked in separate present interviews and receives different replies. At Daxiu Zhu’s hall, an attendant asks why the matter still feels like bereavement after it is understood. The teacher challenges that claim, and the attendant asks directly what the great matter is. Daxiu sends him to sweep the floor. At Lianfeng’s evening memorial gathering, a visitor first asks about the unborn and then about the great matter. Lianfeng answers with head touching heaven and feet standing on earth before addressing a further memorial question. In Zongbao Daodu’s record, a monk repeats the traditional contrast between the matter unexplained and explained, then asks for the great matter itself. The teacher raises a bamboo slat and names it. At another hall, Yangzhuoming asks the assembly what the great matter is, raises his whisk, and says he has hidden nothing from them. The question directs each setting back from abstract certainty to an immediate act.

Senses.Explanation: Four present teachers answer the same high-peak rubric with different material images. At a J28 birthday hall a monk asks a sequence from the four sayings attributed to Gaofeng: earth without grass, sea without fish, great wealth without grain, and awakening without a path. The teacher answers the wealth question that even a thousand mouths would be too few for the rich. In a J37 New Year hall the teacher instead says to eat without chewing even one grain of rice. A J38 teacher tells a questioner that gathered rabbit horns are three feet long, turning the impossible wealth into a further impossibility. Another J38 hall answers with an empty belly and a proud mind, after giving different answers to the earth and sea questions. The four present answers use the same rubric but address separate audiences and occasions.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB415.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miaoyun of Dabei. Miaoyun asks a named interlocutor about great capacity and function, then tests whether the answering shout is one or the other.

Senses.Explanation: A question joins great capacity with its effective use in a Chan encounter. A monk in Tianyin’s assembly quotes a predecessor’s distinction between one who gains great capacity and one who gains great function, then asks about the pair and their reciprocal uses; Tianyin replies with fitting a wedge to a hole and a hat to a head. A monk asks Ruibai Mingxue the full question and hears that not one of thirty blows will be spared. Hanyue Fazang poses the same question in his own verse series and writes of releasing and gathering freely. Miaoyun Zhenxiong asks a named interlocutor the question, receives a shout, and then asks whether that shout was capacity or function. The phrase is tested through different acts, not assigned one fixed definition.

Senses.Explanation: The question is one of Gaofeng’s four linked tests, answered anew in several halls. At a birthday assembly one teacher answers with the moon entering the heart of a wave. Senses.Explanation: A cited Tiantong Xin encounter receives two later responses, while other monks ask the local Tiantong question in live halls. Eryin Mi cites an older monk asking Tiantong Xin what the Tiantong setting is. Xin answers by asking who plants the clouds and who sends the water onward. Eryin contrasts that answer with what he would tell someone asking about his present Daming setting, then asks whether the old and new answers agree. In the Yuan’an Feng record, a monk directly asks about Tiantong’s setting during an evening address. The teacher answers with the height of Taibai Peak and the renown of Linglong Cliff. Pinjixiang’s record also retells the Tiantong Xin exchange, then answers it in a distinct present verse about a difficult song and an empty lute after the king has gone. In the later X85 collection, another monk asks a present teacher the Tiantong question. The teacher replies that there is no place for him to stand, and answers the follow-up about its person with a slap. The shared older encounter, the new verse, and the two live conversations have separate voices and uses.

Yezhu responds with a turtledove calling in a tree while its intent lies in the hemp field. Shanfeng Xian gives an inverted sharp blade whose edge is not shown. Pin Jixiang replies with music from a stringless instrument roaring like thunder. The answers differ sharply, but all occupy the same named place in the band sequence between the curved descending band and the double-lock gold-needle band.

Senses.Explanation: An older three-phrase teaching is recalled and answered anew in two present exchanges. Yunwai Ze discusses old accounts of the three mysteries and three essentials, then quotes Fenyang teaching. In that earlier sequence an unnamed monk asks for the phrase where the learner applies effort and Fenyang answers with an elephant at Jiazhou. Yezhu later receives the same question from a monk in his own hall and answers that it must not be put off until tomorrow. The monk continues by asking for phrases of turning around and closeness. In J35, a different monk asks Huijue Yi the same first question. The teacher says effort starts from letting go and then answers the two follow-up phrases in turn. The repeated question tests three linked parts of a received teaching, while the present replies are not copies of Fenyang old answer.

At one hall a monk asks where to apply effort, and the teacher replies with charging forward to break an enemy. A second teacher answers with securing a boat in swift water. The question is shared, while the present answers and critique differ.

Senses.Explanation: A received three-phrase test is asked anew in several different recorded conversations. Yunwai recounts Fenyang asking for the phrase of exertion, the phrase of turning around, and the phrase of intimacy, then teaches his own assembly through that inherited sequence. In Huijue Yi the present monk asks all three and receives the intimate answer about eating when hungry and sleeping when tired. In Linwo Jian a monk asks the intimate question and the teacher answers with warmth by the fire in cold weather and shade in heat. The continued anthology records a separate monk asking a teacher the same question, who directs him to examine beneath his own heels. The wording remains the questioner voice, while the answers and later teaching differ.

Senses.Explanation: Four teachers answer a question about what is closest to a student in different settings. During a J28 assembly, a monk first asks about exertion and then asks for the student's most intimate point. The teacher replies that few know gratitude and many betray it, before striking at the end of the exchange. In a J29 question period, another monk asks the same short question and receives the answer that one staff blow leaves two marks. A second J29 record quotes an older monk asking Shoushan; Shoushan answers through a seasonal line about spring following winter, and the later commentator says one must stop counting and forget words at the point of closeness. In a J34 hall, a monk moves from exertion to turning and finally asks about intimacy. The teacher redirects him to the very place where he exerts himself, then shouts after the monk tries to settle the matter. The question is shared, while the acts of answering are separate.

Senses.Explanation: Four monks ask about a mountain setting and receive four different local descriptions. In Yinyuan’s spring hall, a monk asks about the mountain scene. The teacher answers that green mountains cover white clouds; when the monk asks who is in the scene, the reply is an aging monk among the clouds. At Yezhu’s hall, another monk asks the same question and hears that sparse bamboo is filled out by smoke and thin plum blossoms by snow. He continues by asking about the person in the scene, and Yezhu describes a clean head and straw sandals underfoot. At Miyin’s opening-of-the-furnace hall, a monk gets snow-resistant pines for the mountain scene and a crescent moon above the sleeping hall for the person. At Gusu Zun’s hall, a fourth monk hears of uneven wild trees before peaks and red and white flowers along the ridge. Gusu then answers the companion person-in-the-scene question with indifference to right and wrong and distance from fame. Each pair of answers belongs to a separate live exchange.

In a J27 question sequence, an unnamed monk asks about Kunlun on an elephant led by an egret; the teacher answers with an iron bar stretching ten thousand miles. A J28 interlocutor poses the same image in another exchange and hears that there is a cause precisely where no cause seems to be. A J37 teacher uses the same short direction but continues with a different local reply. Senses.Explanation: Four questioners bring Gaofeng’s stone-tiger prompt to different teachers and receive different replies. The old four-question set attributed to Gaofeng includes a mud ox carrying the moon, a stone tiger holding its cub, an iron snake entering an adamantine eye, and Kunlun riding an elephant. In J27 a monk asks the tiger question after the mud-ox prompt; the teacher says an iron whip cannot drive it up. In J28 the layman Wuji Zhang asks a different teacher and receives a warning against claws and teeth. In J34 a monk asks for Gaofeng’s four sayings, but the teacher declines to explain the stone tiger for him and asks for the monk’s own answer; the monk shifts to the donor’s meal. In J35 another monk presses the same question, hears that daybreak has come without knowing daylight, and the teacher later makes a tiger sound. The four exact prompts belong to different present questioners, while the answers show four distinct teaching moves.

Senses.Explanation: A monk asks for the ordinary nonbirth line, the first of a three-line teaching, and four teachers respond with words or gestures of their own. Yunwai Xingze answers a monk’s first-line question by saying he drags it across and pulls it straight; when pressed, he says the monk can neither seek life nor seek death. Wenmu Nian sets the first line beside the subtle impartial and clear-essence lines, answering with grass growing from stone and an unmoving cloud hidden by the mountain; his later hall address draws the sequence together. In Shanduo Zhenzai’s dialogue, the source-named monk Huizhao asks the first line after requesting a direct response; Shanduo says a mouth cannot say it, then answers the second and third lines differently. Zhufeng Zhenxu responds to the first question by looking upward, then looks downward for the second and strikes his staff and shouts for the third. The fixed first-line question allows the reader to compare distinct answers without treating the three lines as interchangeable.

Senses.Explanation: Three different questioners use this Three Barriers question and receive different replies. In Duanyu Zhi’s Jiaxing record, the Chan practitioner Jintan from Tiantong first asks about the teacher’s birth connection, then asks how his own hand resembles the Buddha’s. Duanyu answers that the stars turn toward the north and all waters flow east; Jintan continues with the foot and birth-connection questions. In Henglulin’s hall, a lay official Wang asks about the meaning of Huanglong’s Three Barriers after another monk has asked about ordinary and holy people. He puts the exact hand question, and the teacher answers that feeling for one’s nose makes one lose one’s mouth. In Zhufeng Min’s record, an unnamed monk asks the same question amid a list of Chan teaching questions. Zhufeng replies with an image of mountains shaking and a poet’s wild freedom. The shared line is a received testing question; the local speakers and responses are distinct.
