Senses.Explanation: A line from Dongshan’s snake-and-frog case becomes a live test in three settings. In the older case a monk asks Dongshan whether to rescue a frog caught by a snake. Dongshan says rescuing leaves both eyes unable to see, while not rescuing leaves no form or shadow. A J26 teacher quotes that response and asks a monk what rescue means. After rejecting the monk’s answer, he tests the assembly and finally gives his own line about a flower without showy color. In J39 a different monk asks the same question in a live exchange; the teacher answers with the image of a different tuning on a moving string, then answers the paired not-rescue question with falling leaves. A J40 teacher cites the J26 exchange and its verse, judges the earlier teacher’s solution, and offers a new answer about a red sun returning to an ancient cave. The inherited rescue formula supports three separate tests.

Senses.Explanation: Three live hall questioners and Su Dongpo ask who inhabits a scene, with answers shaped by each setting. At a hall requested by a military governor, a questioner asks Tian’an Sheng for the Faqing scene and then asks who is in it. Tian’an replies with a description of a vigorous soldier and a defender of the lords. During a Huguo tea talk, another monk asks the Huguo teacher about the local scene and then the person within it. The teacher first gives green pine and bamboo, then answers that the person is seven long and eight short. In Baichi’s New Year’s hall, a monk asks about the new-year scene and hears of color overflowing the woods. He asks the exact person-in-the-scene question and receives a reply about thousands coming and going. Chuiwan’s record then recounts Su Dongpo, also called Zizhan, testing the courtesan Qin Cao with questions about a lake scene, the person within it, and its meaning. Qin Cao answers the exact question with a skirt like Xiang River water and hair piled like Wushan clouds. Chuiwan later imagines an alternate exchange, but the selected exact line is Su’s question in the retold encounter. The term is a question whose scene changes from governor’s hall to monastery, New Year, and lake conversation.

Senses.Explanation: A question about the time before birth draws three different replies. At a birthday sermon a monk asks the question and the teacher points to the top of a peak turned upside down. Another monk asks in a separate hall and hears that the teacher has never studied together with him; the next question about after birth gets the opposite reply. A third teacher puts the question to an assembly and, after a pause, answers with the ordinary acts of dressing and eating. The three settings move from a pointed image to a personal exchange and a public teaching.

Senses.Explanation: A lay visitor, a young seeker, and two monks ask for a face before birth. During tea with a J29 teacher, Layman Shen asks about the face before birth. The teacher raises a round fruit, repeats the gesture for after birth and for the interval between, then warns the amused visitor against a false claim of understanding. In the biography within Baiyu recorded sayings, the young Baiyu goes to Bianshan Ruibai Xue and asks the exact question; Bianshan answers with a staff blow, and the encounter leads into Baiyu later training. A J38 monk asks the question and receives a turtle facing a fire. When he shouts, the teacher says the shout is his present face and presses the earlier question again. In a J39 birthday hall, a monk asks the same question and Konggu Daocheng answers with turtle hair propping open the sky. These are four distinct asking scenes, with different questioners and responses.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask teachers for the original body; a fourth source quotes an older answer and critiques it. A monk asks Zhaozhou for the original body. Zhaozhou says that since he came to know the old monk, this very person has not become someone else; he rejects the monk’s attempted conclusion about separation. In Buhui’s hall, a different monk receives a paradox about length and width. When he says he did not ask about that body, Buhui points to his own six-foot form, then shouts after the monk calls it illusory. At Yunwai Ze’s hall, a third monk asks and hears a great mountain’s height; the teacher’s follow-up says half is within the water and half outside it. Huigong’s record quotes an older monk asking Yuwang about the original body and Yuwang replying that it is seen in reflected light. Huigong objects that this sends the monk to work among shadows and proposes a different appraisal. The quotation and critique make a fourth deployment while retaining the older questioner’s voice.

Senses.Explanation: The bridge-and-water paradox is posed in three different live sequences of four linked questions. At a J28 birthday hall, a monk asks about carrying a hoe with empty hands, riding an ox while walking, and a person crossing a bridge. He ends by asking how the bridge flows while the water does not; Faxi Yin tells him to look directly down. In a J37 exchange, a different monk follows the same sequence and Shending Yikui answers the bridge question by saying people invert things, lose themselves and chase objects. In an X72 exchange, a third monk asks the sequence in another hall and the teacher answers with a short rope passing through flames. The repeated paradox has three different respondents and three different ways of testing it.

Senses.Explanation: A line from the Lotus Sutra prompts three distinct questions or teacher challenges about the one matter. At a small address requested by layman Li Songting, Sanshan Lai cites the Lotus Sutra line that only one matter is true and two others are not. He asks what that one matter is, pauses, and says he does not know how to add a snake foot before speaking of the layman journey and a verse. In Liangting Ting record, layman Ying Siyin quotes the same Lotus Sutra line and asks the one-matter question. Liangting answers by snapping his fingers. In a Yushan hall, an unnamed questioner also quotes the scripture and asks what the one matter is. Yushan answers with an image of an official office closing early, then challenges the monk later claim and strikes him. The shared scriptural source is inherited; the three present deployments differ in who asks and how the teacher answers.

Senses.Explanation: An older question about the Vairocana seal is criticized twice, while two present monks ask for the seal directly. Jie’an Jin cites an older monk’s question to Furi Bi about the Vairocana seal. Furi answers that straw sandals tread through snow, leaving a trace at every step. A previous commentator offers a different reply; Jie’an says the old masters raised the seal yet used the wrong words, and supplies his own counter-answer about the question and response themselves. At Yuquan Lianyue Zheng’s hall, a present monk asks the exact question. Lianyue raises a fist and says it has neither writing nor characters, then strikes with his staff when the monk asks about light at its tip. At Hanxiu’s retirement hall, another monk asks after a line about raising the formless Vairocana seal. Hanxiu replies with the frost on a plank bridge, then warns the monk against fastening on the answer. The Xiangyan record cites the same old straw-sandals exchange as Jie’an’s source. Its current commentator criticizes the old reply, says the seal predates birth, and would answer a new question with a slap. These are two distinct live questions and two distinct present comments on one older encounter.

Senses.Explanation: Three visitors ask about the moon reflected in water and receive different answers. Monastic officer Shi first asks Shanhui about a flower in a mirror and hears that it stings the eyes from every side. He follows by asking what the moon in the water is. Shanhui replies that searching sky and earth with a scoop cannot make it whole; after a further question he shouts. In Yezhu's record, an unnamed monk asks what the moon in the water is. Yezhu says the monk cannot scoop or grasp it. At a Huijue Yi hall, a monk asks only about the moon in the water. Huijue says the full one is full and the missing one missing, then deals separately with a mirror image. The same image becomes three different local tests.

Senses.Explanation: A question about the Fayan school appears within live examinations of the five Chan houses. An unnamed questioner asks Miyin about the Fayan school after asking about Guiyang, and Miyin replies that the same principle sends growth across mountains and rivers. In Pofeng Puchong’s room, Pofeng himself asks the monastery director the same question; the director answers with grass, trees, tiles, and stones. Another questioner asks Lianfeng, who responds that what falls away is no other thing. Yuquan Qibai Fu answers a fourth questioner with an arrow point and empty walls. The records place this category among questions about the other houses, but each is a separate exchange with its own speaker and response.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask the same object riddle within different lists and receive different concrete images. A monk questions Miyin about a series of impossible objects, including a stringless zither, bottomless boat, flute without holes and basket without a bottom. Miyin answers the basket question by saying fish and dragons are kept from reaching the Yangtze, then addresses a further question about a seamless pagoda. Another monk asks Hansong Zhicao a related sequence. Hansong answers that one should not kill a dead snake but carry it home carefully in the bottomless basket; when the monk praises the response, Hansong strikes him. In a third exchange, a monk asks Meixi Du about a bottomless boat and bowl before the basket. Meixi says it can be carried from the green ridge loaded with mountain flowers, then answers questions about other impossible objects. The same riddle draws three unrelated images from the three current teachers.

Senses.Explanation: Three live questioners and one written question series ask about a bottomless bowl and receive different images. At Miyin’s hall, a questioner works through a sequence of “without” objects, including the country without action, a scaleless balance, and a rootless tree. For the bottomless bowl, the teacher answers by asking who carries it back and forth. At Hansong Cao’s hall, a monk asks the same series; Hansong answers the bowl question with a vessel lifted to swallow heaven and earth and opened to restrain a poisonous dragon. Jifei’s written set titled the ten things without presents the exact question in a compact question-and-answer list. Its answer says that mountains are stored and the sea is contained. At Dongshan Meixi Du’s hall, a questioner asks about a bottomless boat and then the bowl. The teacher answers that it is filled with fragrant rice to feed people and heavenly beings. These are local uses of one stock series, with different replies rather than one repeated bowl image.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask about a country of nonaction and receive three different images. In the Miyin record, a monk asks a series of questions about impossible objects and states, including the country of nonaction. Miyin says that neither sage nor ordinary person rests inside it, then continues with answers about a starless scale, rootless tree and bottomless bowl. In another hall, a monk first asks Pofeng Chong about the country of action and hears of the high sky and aligned creatures. He then asks about the country of nonaction, and Pofeng answers with the wide sea and tides from a hundred rivers. A third monk puts the question to Hansong Zhicao in another list of paradoxical objects. Hansong answers with a verse of singing through ages of sage rule and joy across vast distances. The same short question enters three distinct teaching sequences.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher and three monks put the same unconditioned-dharma question into different live teaching settings. Guxue Zhenzhe first cites a verse by Zhu Xi about reading Buddhist books and understanding the unconditioned dharma. He then asks his assembly what that dharma is, raises his staff, and answers with a couplet about a winter poem and writing that reaches the four seas. In Fangrong Xi’s address, a monk asks the question after a remark that sages differ through the unconditioned dharma. Xi answers by postponing the long explanation until tomorrow. At Zizhou Chuan’s release-of-retreat address, a monk asks about conditioned dharmas and then asks the unconditioned question. The teacher replies with green mountains reaching the sky, and the monk falls silent. At Miyin’s year-end hall, a monk contrasts conditioned and unconditioned dharmas. The teacher first answers with the sound of stopping an echo, then answers the exact question with bare hands and empty fists. The shared wording leads to a raised staff and verse, a postponement, a mountain image, and a bare-handed reply.

Senses.Explanation: The stringless zither appears in a live exchange, a written answer list, and another live exchange. At Guangfu, a monk asks the Miyin teacher a succession of questions about objects with impossible features: a rootless tree, a bottomless bowl, and a zither without strings. The teacher answers the exact question by saying its natural, clear resonance has few listeners who understand it. In Jifei’s written list headed “The Ancients’ Ten Nothings,” the same question appears between the bottomless bowl and the flute without holes, with the answer “a thousand peaks lean an ear.” The text presents it as an item in a written question-and-answer series, not as a new monk standing before the teacher. At Dongshan, a monk asks Meixi Du about the same impossible zither in a live question sequence. Meixi answers with the enduring resonance of high mountains and flowing water, then challenges the monk over the ten items. The differing response frames give the recurring question three local uses.

Senses.Explanation: Four records ask the same question in separate exchanges and answer with age, shapes, a strike, and a verse. A monk in Zhaozhou’s record asks what the mystery within the mystery is. Zhaozhou turns to the age of a monk he has in mind, withholding the expected formula. In Wolong Zishui’s hall, another questioner works through the three mysteries. Wolong answers the final question with a pointed water-chestnut, three corners and a fork. At a Yezhu hall, a monk asks the sequence and the teacher strikes him for the deepest mystery, then says the begging bowl is asking for wine money. In Yuechuang Liao’s hall, a further monk receives a blow followed by a verse that breaks the number five into three and turns a chicken into a hawk. The shared question invites different acts and images in each record.

Senses.Explanation: Four local halls answer the Yuquan-scene question with different visible features and actions. At Yuquan Lianyue Zheng’s hall, a monk asks about the Yuquan setting and hears of pearl water below a deep-blue mountain. He asks next who is in that setting, and the teacher answers that a clap brings up pearls. Yuechuang Liao’s record preserves another question about Yuquan; the teacher answers with Wanshou Mountain and the measure of heaven and earth, then answers the companion person question with seeing and hearing. In the Huayan Buyan Le record’s Yuquan hall, a questioner asks the exact question after the teacher’s incense offering. The teacher replies with yellow leaves on five peaks and a belt of green pine, then answers the next question with a white staff repeatedly raised. In Yuquan Qibai Fu’s own hall, a questioner hears of green willows before the courtyard and red fallen flowers behind the steps. The four halls attach distinct local images to the same place-name question.

Senses.Explanation: This question names one specified belt in Fushan’s nine-belt scheme and asks a present teacher to demonstrate it. A monk asks Faxiyin through Fushan’s nine belts one by one. For the belt of principle and phenomena crossing freely, Faxiyin replies with a bee carrying flower matter home and a butterfly turning through a grassy path. Yezhu Fuhui answers the same named category with a fallen blossom drifting where spring does not govern it. Shenfeng Xian uses the image of an ingenuous cloth bag in the crossroads. Yuan’an Feng answers with an eight-sided millstone moving in empty space, and the monk later challenges the whole set of answers. These are four present question-and-answer sequences about one category in a named Chan taxonomy; their different images are not four definitions imported from a doctrinal manual.

Senses.PreferredTarget: what did Bodhidharma come from the West for?
AlternateTargets: what is the meaning of Bodhidharma's coming from the West?
SearchAliases: why did Bodhidharma come from India
meaning of the ancestral teacher's arrival
Senses.Explanation: “What did Bodhidharma come from the West for?” is a fixed public-interview question about what the ancestral teacher's west-to-east coming amounted to. The question is a lexical object in its own right, separate from the sharply different answers and actions that follow it. An unnamed monk asks Zhaozhou Congshen and receives the cypress in the courtyard; multiple later works preserve that inherited family, but it counts as one encounter. Elsewhere an unnamed monk receives Chan Master Dawei's promise to answer after turning around at Fanxian Mountain. Ding Shangzuo asks it and Linji Yixuan descends, seizes him, and demands that he speak; Longya Judun asks Linji and is told to pass over the Chan bench before Linji strikes. Wuzu Fayan actively reuses the formula while pressing Yuanwu Keqin about the cypress, and Fayun Xiu proposes “verbal fall” as the reply if someone asks him. The varied responses establish the stability of the question, not a menu of meanings for it.
Senses.Note: Bodhidharma is the ancestral teacher conventionally invoked by this formula. Cypress, bench, blow, demand, and other responses belong to their own turns and must not be folded into the question's translation.

Senses.Explanation: Four teachers raise the barrier question in their own halls and answer through gesture, images, or another question. Feiyin’s hall moves from clouds, running water, grass, and birds to the claim that there is no teaching outside these things. He asks what the patriarchs’ barrier is, traces a cross with his whisk, and challenges the assembly to identify it before citing an older Yangqi encounter. Fushi asks the same question at a birthday hall requested by a lay supporter. He strikes his whisk and responds with cool water running by stones and wind carrying fragrance through flowers. Guxue speaks to an opening retreat about the urgency of birth and death, asks what the barrier is, and postpones his explanation until the listeners break their own lacquer buckets. Shuijian Hai’s hall says one must pass the barrier to enter, asks what it is, then invokes Zhaozhou’s testing of a woman and asks who pierced whose nose. Each present teacher uses the question for a separate audience and purpose.

Senses.Explanation: A monk asks a teacher to identify the source from which all phenomena arise. A monk asks Zhaozhou Congshen the question during a sequence of exchanges and receives the answer “beams and rafters”; he says he does not understand. Senses.Explanation: Four monks cite the same older verse and ask separate teachers what can preside over the myriad appearances. At a memorial hall requested by a lay patron, a monk quotes the verse about something prior to heaven and earth that can be lord of myriad appearances and not fade with the seasons. Feiyin Tongrong answers his exact question by warning him not to see with the eyes, then gives a further verse and plants his staff. At Yun’e Xi’s birthday hall, another monk recites the same verse. Yun’e raises his staff, asks whether the monk understands, and strikes when the monk hesitates. In the Shending hall, a third monk asks with the verse and receives the instruction to set his gaze high; when he thanks the teacher, Shending presses him with images of a decoy pigeon and a wren holding a cold branch. At a Hongshan hall, a fourth monk asks and hears that the mountain is high and the road long. The monk offers a verse about touching the nose of empty space, and the teacher strikes him. The four live questions quote one inherited verse, but their teacher responses differ sharply.

Senses.Explanation: Four monks ask the same doctrinal question and receive four very different Chan answers. Chulin’s interlocutor asks about empty, nonempty, and then both empty and nonempty Tathagata treasury; the teacher raises a bamboo slip and asks what the monk calls it. In Defeng’s record another monk reaches the same third question after two blows, and the teacher strikes his staff, warning against grasping its name. Miaoyun’s respondent moves through bottomless bowl and covered Yellow River before answering the combined question with a stone mortar and wind. In a separate X68 exchange, the teacher turns all three questions toward eating and sleeping, then rebukes the monk for failing to understand those ordinary acts. Four similar prompts yield four independent present responses.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask about the empty tathāgata store and receive different images or challenges. In a J37 hall, a monk asks about ordinary and sacred people meeting. He then asks about the empty tathāgata store, and Foyuan answers with the sun uncovered and burning across the world. At another J37 early talk, a monk asks Chulin the same question; Chulin asks what the monk said, then treats questions about the nonempty and jointly empty-nonempty store in turn. An X68 collection records a separate monk asking a teacher the same doctrinal question after questions about the Buddha bodies. The teacher answers that one eats until full and sleeps. The three answers turn a doctrinal label toward light, an immediate challenge, and ordinary bodily activity.

Senses.Explanation: Five monks ask for the first principle; a sixth teacher raises the question to his own assembly. At Yangzhuo Ming’s hall, a monk asks for the first principle. The teacher strikes his staff, asks whether the assembly heard, and continues that ears can fail to hear while a mouth says nothing. Fushi tells a different monk that the request is empty argument; when the monk asks why, he says words have no real meaning and shouts. Tian’an Sheng is asked the question after a sequence about what remains unbroken. He replies that he has already answered. Eryin Mi tells another monk that the very question has fallen into a second meaning, then strikes him after a shout. At an opening hall Tan’an asks rhetorically what the first principle is and turns to pines, birds, flowers, wind, and moon. In Konggu Daocheng’s hall, a monk asks the same question. Konggu pauses, asks if he understands, and says the monk’s claim has fallen into the second meaning. The answers differ in gesture, refusal, and image.

Senses.Explanation: A questioner asks the respondent to demonstrate the first of the three essentials associated with Linji's three mysteries and three essentials. Across six independent records, the question appears inside a serial public exchange: the questioner asks for each mystery and then each essential in order. The replies differ sharply, including 'myriad differences are all illuminated in one light,' news of an amnesty, a returning night boat, 'opening your mouth is already laughable,' Yama's karmic mirror, and a wooden hawk flying through the sky. The stable dictionary unit is therefore the test-question itself, not any one reply.

Senses.Explanation: Six questioners work through the three mysteries and receive different replies at the second. Miyun answers a monk’s second-mystery question with the roundness of the head and squareness of the feet. Tianyin instead takes up his staff and lays it across the table. Shiqi offers a lone goose dropping toward the river ahead. Muyun presses his staff against the monk’s mouth and warns of piercing his lips. At Yinyuan’s hall, West Hall Wude asks a sequence after a retreat. Yinyuan says that touching the second mystery loses half of it. Longguang Dafu answers a further monk that a penalty follows even after the blow. Each answer belongs to a separate present exchange. The fixed question marks a position in the three mysteries while the response can be a bodily image, a gesture, or an immediate rebuke.

Senses.Explanation: Monks take the second line of Pang Yun’s gathering verse as a live question, and four teachers answer it differently in hall dialogues. Pang Yun’s verse says the ten directions assemble, everyone studies nonaction, this is the place to choose a Buddha, and an empty mind returns successful. At a late consultation a monk asks Tianan Sheng what each line does for people; Tianan answers the nonaction question by pointing to the monk’s own idleness. At the opening of a retreat, a monk works through the four lines with Lianyue Daozheng, who answers this one by saying there is no other matter and then presses the assembly about dropping distinctions. In Yunsou Benzhu’s hall another monk asks each line; Yunsou answers this one with swallowing a thorny chestnut and passing through a diamond ring. At the winter release a monk presents the same sequence to Yikui Yuankui; Yikui replies by asking what the monk had been doing before, and pushes back when the exchange continues. The headword is the monk’s question about the verse, while Pang Yun remains its quoted author.

Senses.Explanation: An older monk's question to Benren draws four different later readings of sound and color. Baishui Benren says he does not wish to toy with people through phrases before sound or beyond color, because sound is not sound and color is not color. An unnamed monk asks what sound that is not sound means. Benren replies by asking whether one can call it color; a matching question about color gets the converse answer. A J25 teacher quotes this dialogue and tests whether his assembly can understand sound and color without obstruction. A J28 commentator considers Benren's answer too shallow and answers the two questions with birds in a bare tree and spring color in blossoms. One J34 teacher raises the exchange in a short talk, asks why Benren replied with color to a question about sound, and warns against the easy victory of a general. Another J34 poet cites Benren along with Xuedou's older comment, then composes a separate verse about seeing, speaking, and grasping without handles. The old questioner remains unnamed in all four records.

Senses.Explanation: Four five-eye teachings begin with the same question but give different local answers. In Hongjue Min’s hall, an unnamed questioner begins a sequence on the five eyes with the fleshly eye. The teacher strikes and calls him an ignorant lump, then answers the next four eye questions differently. Tian’an Sheng receives the same question after one about the dharma eye; he replies that the questioner falls short of him, then reverses their positions when asked about the correct eye. In Yezhu’s teaching, a lay visitor begins a five-eye series, and the teacher tells him to look beneath his eyebrows and feet; the exchange ends with the teacher inviting him to tea. Yi’an later recounts a question someone asked him the previous day and gives his one-syllable answer to each of the five eyes before offering a verse on each. The headword names the ordinary eye within the five-eye scheme, while each teacher uses the list as a live teaching device.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask about Linji's use and receive restraint, a strike, and a martial image. At a hall marking repayment of his teacher's kindness, a monk asks Zhikong Yun about the first meaning, then Linji's device and use. Zhikong says he has a staff but will not strike the monk, then warns him not to let the moment pass. In Meixi Du's record, another monk asks first about Linji's device and is struck. He asks about Linji's use and is struck again; after bowing he is pressed on whether he recognizes device and use. In Yongjue Yuanxian's record, a monk asks about Linji's illumination and hears that a rhinoceros light leaves no ghost hidden. He then asks about use and receives an image of brandishing a spear to settle peace. These are three separate teacher responses to the same short question.

Senses.Explanation: A teacher or questioner asks for a phrase fitting the moment of departure. Yuan’an Liao puts the question in his own ritual address and answers with leaving the Saha realm and appearing in a lotus realm as he raises the fire. When Shanduo Zhenzai is about to travel to Longxing, a monk asks him for the phrase, and he answers that Longxing is two hundred li away. At Ziyong Ru’s departure address, a questioner asks with a poem about the journey; Ziyong replies with a red-leaf image and a reluctance to cut paper. These three present uses place the phrase in actual departures, but the ritual speaker in the first source is the question’s utterer, unlike the monks in the other two.

Senses.Explanation: Three new-year exchanges ask who belongs to the old year. In Poshan's new-year hall, a monk first asks about a person of the new year and receives an image of rouge and powder. He then asks about the person of the old year. Poshan answers with a dust-covered face and goes on to compare old and new. In Linye Tongqi's record, a visitor asks the same pair of questions. Linye says the new-year person wears a patched robe and the old-year person wears a hat. The monk then offers fruit and leaves embarrassed after the teacher challenges him. In Miyin's new-year hall, a monk asks about the new-year scene and hears of leaves and fresh growth. His follow-up about the old-year person receives an image of watching fish in shallow water and birds in light mist. The calendrical contrast becomes a different response in each present hall.

Senses.Explanation: A direct old answer and later critiques press the question of awakening beyond a settled definition. An unnamed questioner asks Zhaozhou what bodhi is; Zhaozhou answers by pointing to an icchantika, someone thought beyond awakening. In a later record, Zizhou Chuan quotes a monk putting the question to Deshan. Deshan strikes and orders him out, and Zizhou comments that the teacher’s severity may have been generous to a monk who missed it. Juelang, speaking with a learned visitor about how to investigate a case, turns a scriptural line about the restless mind’s cessation into a run of questions: what is restlessness, how does it cease, and what is bodhi? He asks whether it was always present or newly gained. A lamp records another direct encounter: a monk asks Shangfang Qiyue the question and receives the answer “bricks and tiles,” followed by a further terse reply. The four settings do not offer one fixed definition.

Senses.Explanation: An old question about the western arrival is preserved with different later responses. One source quotes a monk asking Fadeng the question and receiving the single word bitter, then offers its own verse. Three others retell the encounter in which Baofang asks Taigang or Yifeng and is seized as the teacher steps down from his seat. Their present verses use different images of thunder, a rising tide, and awakening. The fourth source also adds a direct current judgment on the force of that teacher’s method. These are source-local versions of an inherited test with separate later readings.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask the same striking question and receive three different replies. In J39 a monk asks a series of Dongshan style questions, including the dry-bones song, and the teacher replies with a bell biting through the sea tongue and a pillar rising into moonlight. Senses.Explanation: Literally, this asks, ‘Where do the buddhas emerge?’ It is a stable encounter question rather than the name of a place. Yuanwu Keqin records the unnamed monk's question to Yunmen Wenyan and Yunmen's answer, ‘East Mountain walks on water.’ In Dahui Zonggao's recollection, Yuanwu raises that exchange and gives a different answer: ‘A warm wind comes from the south; a slight coolness enters the palace halls.’ The Five Lamps Compendium preserves a separate exchange with Master Lingkan of Western Sichuan, who answers, ‘Emergence has nothing to do with buddhas; when spring comes, grass greens by itself.’ The differing answers do not change the wording or grammatical referent of the question.

Senses.Explanation: Three local questioners ask about Zhaozhou’s tea and receive answers shaped by their own encounters. In Juelang Sheng’s tea talk, the named visitor Huang Jingshou asks whether Fushan tea can serve everyone and whether it has any flavor. After the teacher answers, Huang asks what Zhaozhou’s tea is. Juelang replies that Lu Tong would not drink it, and the dialogue moves to what happens afterward. In Baishan Dekai’s hall, a monk asks about Zhaozhou’s tea after questions on killing sword and life-giving sword. Baishan says one cannot do without a cup after a meal, then answers a separate question about Jinniu’s rice. In the Anheidou collection, a monk asks the same exact question after asking about Yunmen’s cake. The local teacher replies that it does not wet the mouth, and the monk then asks about the patriarch’s coming from the West. All three invoke the remembered Zhaozhou tea motif while the actual answers belong to three different scenes.

Senses.Explanation: The question asks about a movement in the Chan language of merit and position. One teacher poses it himself to a visitor in a sequence of tests, and the visitor warns against trampling everyone. In three other halls monks ask the question and receive very different answers: a request to speak again, an image of white clouds entering a valley, and a remark that this hall does not follow other places. Each exchange continues into related questions about turning back from position to merit and about the two together. The headword remains the initial question, while its questioner and answer are local to each source.

Senses.Explanation: A question seeks a phrase for the turn that changes one’s position in the encounter. A monk asks Shaweng Huihai after asking about a phrase that meets the situation; Shaweng answers with a verse about crossing the Dragon Gate and stirring a fresh wind. At a funeral rite Foyuan Chegang asks what phrase marks the deceased monk’s turning, casts the torch, and says “Burn.” Jingting Dezong tests a monk after telling him a road’s end still calls for a turn; he asks for the phrase and the monk answers with the four directions, leading to a further test. The words join a formal dialogue, a funeral act, and a living exchange.

Senses.Explanation: A monk asks for the phrase that discerns a Chan practitioner, usually immediately after asking how a beginner is received. Sanfeng Zang answers the discernment question by saying that words do not depend on the tongue and silence still calls for an apt expression. Lingyin Wen gives the short challenge “Do you understand?”, then answers the next request for a proper command with a blade image. Baishan Kai replies with a wooden horse neighing into the wind and an iron ox drinking the western river, after his prior answer about receiving a beginner. Fenyang Wude answers that the sun rises in the west, then continues through the other requested phrases and says the four turns test monks as they come forward. In every record the question is voiced by a present questioner; the teacher’s reply tests discernment in that exchange rather than defining all monks with one formula.

Senses.Explanation: A monk asks how Mahakasyapa can hear without hearing, usually immediately after asking how the Buddha speaks without speaking. In Shiqi Tongyun’s hall, a monk asks first about the Buddha’s speech without speaking and then this question about Mahakasyapa. Shiqi tells him to try reciting the next line, strikes him after a further question about sight and hearing, and strikes again when the monk persists. Baichi Xingyuan responds to the same paired question by asking whether the senior monk is deaf; after the monk offers a celebratory line, Baichi challenges that answer too. Lianyue Daozheng answers the second question with “two flaps of skin for ears” and then says the point is plain and distinct. Yunwai Xingze gives a deliberately different response, about Amitabha receiving someone in the west, before moving to other questions. The clause is the monk’s test question in each scene, not a claim that Mahakasyapa literally lacked hearing or a fixed answer shared by the teachers.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB446.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lingyin Wen. A monk asks Lingyin Wen about Huilong and hears of lotus leaves, reed blossoms, wind and a boat.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks ask about Huilong's setting and hear different images of water and mountains. At a retreat-opening hall in the Buhui record, a monk asks about Huilong's landscape. The teacher answers that reeds cover both banks like woven brocade while peaks surround the place. The monk then asks about the person within that landscape, and the teacher supplies another image. In a Miyin hall, a different monk asks the same first question. Miyin points to two clear rivers meeting at a crossing, then answers the follow-up about the person there with a boat under wind and moonlight. In Lingyin Wen's record, a monk asks the same place question and receives an image of rain warming lotus leaves and wind stirring reed blossoms like snow on a boat. That teacher continues with a different response about the person in the landscape. Huilong is approached through three separate local dialogues, not a single repeated scenic description.

Senses.Explanation: What is the phrase that threads through the truth-body — the school's standing demand for the word that goes through rather than points, asked of Yunmen and answered with the Dipper, then ruled, re-answered, versed, and smuggled for five hundred years. The origin, in Yunmen Wenyan's own catechism. Question after question runs the gauntlet — the Yunmen sword: the ancestor; the birthplace of all buddhas: ask me another; the white ox in the open: the confronting cue that changes no road. Then: what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? The master: hide the body in the Dipper. And next after: what is the original school? Not asking, not answering. Dahui Zonggao raises the exchange in the hall and rules on it: the old man of Yunmen, answering thus, answered only the truth-body phrase — he did not answer the phrase that threads through. If today someone asked Jingshan, what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body — I would tell him: a night-market opened in a midge's eye, a swing swung on a great tiger's tongue. And Miyun Yuanwu, raising both at the Tongxuan temple, turns it a third way: if anyone asks me what the threading-through phrase is — a staff across the spine on the spot; even if he does not understand, I guarantee he will not forget it for a whole eternity. The other line of the family: a monk asks Bajiao Huiqing, what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? Bajiao: first, you may not ask; second, you may not rest. The monk: I do not understand. Bajiao: come a third time and I will meet you. Touzi Yiqing verses it: ask not of Vimalakirti lying ill within the city; Vulture Peak idly shuts away its light. To cross the flowing sands is without difficulty — only do not hear the oriole crying in that grove. And Daxiu Zhu, raising the same at the Buddha-birthday hall and versing: not asking, not resting — the truth-body is not on the tip of the tongue; but let the third coming bring the meeting, and it will run the Guishan water-buffalo to death. Yuejiang Zhengyin, in his own hall catechism at Dianshan: what is the birthplace of all buddhas? Is the Dianshan lake full yet? What is the blow-hair sword? Dust rising from a well-bottom. What is the white ox in the open? Hewing the forehead, gazing toward Caoxi. And what is the phrase that threads through the truth-body? That smuggler of private salt. Then he turns on the assembly: under white sun and blue sky, dreamers with open eyes are as hemp and millet — bring me the dream-thing to look at. You see me talk thus and say the old man talks in his sleep — but when you are not dreaming, what is the thing before your eyes? And Eryin Mi, picking old cases: the elder Fulang, meeting the questioner's line at Yunmen's gate — the master hid the body in the Dipper; Fulang could not fathom it and pressed further. Yunmen gripped him: Speak, speak! Fulang hesitated; the master pushed him away and gave a verse — the cloud-gate tower sheers off the low white clouds; fish in rushing water dare not rest; entering the gate, your seeing was already known — why trouble to lift the rutting mud again? Fulang woke whole. Gripped and pushed away, rolling whole-bodied through the grass; the verse retold, the tongue dragging on the ground — yet the elder who opened an eye right there, says Eryin, is still only a lacquer bucket.

Senses.Explanation: What is the Way? is a recurring public-interview question. Zhaozhou Congshen asks Nanquan Puyuan and receives “ordinary mind is the Way.” Li Ao asks Yaoshan Weiyan, who points upward and then to a water jar. A quoted monk asks Shitou Xiqian and receives “wood,” while another quoted monk asks Xingshan Weikuan and receives “a fine mountain.” The same question opens distinct encounters with unlike answers.

Senses.Explanation: An unfinished half becomes a live question and two teachers' rhetorical challenges. At a small address in the Xuzhou Sheng record requested by lay supporters, a monk offers a verse about roads through the green willows. Xuzhou says the monk has spoken only half. The monk asks what the other half is, and Xuzhou returns the task to him: that half is his to say. At a midautumn hall Wuzhun speaks of everyone admiring the full moon while he still finds it half missing. He asks what that other half is and says he will tell them when the moon rises in the west. At an opening-of-retreat hall Gulin Qingmao holds a staff and says even his claim of freeing the assembly from bonds is only half. He asks about the other half, strikes the staff, and answers with the wideness of heaven and earth. The question tests completion in three distinct teaching moments.

Senses.Explanation: The question of the other side is posed by three teachers and a monk in distinct hall encounters. Chaozong works through seeing mountains and waters in three ways, warning that each fixed position can become another trap. He asks his assembly what the matter on the other side is, gives a shout, and answers by warning against injuring an uninjured place. At Shiguan’s opening-of-retreat hall, a monk first asks about the matter over there. Shiguan answers by asking the exact other-side question back to him; the monk shouts, and the teacher asks him to try another shout before striking him. In Baishan Kai’s small address, the teacher calls a monk forward and says to understand the other-side matter while carrying on this-side conduct. Baishan then asks the exact question and hears the monk answer that an iron ox walks on water. After more exchanges, Baishan coughs and says the performance has collapsed. In Zhufeng Min’s hall, a monk asks the exact question and gets an image of a bird unable to pass and water unable to leak through. He follows with the this-side question and receives another pair of images. The wording tests a local exchange rather than naming one fixed place.

Senses.Explanation: This question asks a teacher to show what an indestructible adamantine body means in the present encounter. An unnamed monk asks Yinyuan Longqi what the indestructible body is. Yinyuan raises a foot and asks whether this very thing can be destroyed, turning the question back on the monk. Guxue Zhenzhe asks a sick monk the same question, rejects the monk’s attempted answer, and when the monk asks it back, points to the boil by his buttock. Governor Zhou asks Shuijian Hai the question during a visit; Shuijian raises his whisk, and when Zhou asks for direct pointing, gives a local-distance answer instead. A monk asks Hanyu Hongxian, who replies with green mountains and waters; the monk then cites the claim that all forms are illusory and asks where the transmitted robe can be placed. Across the four scenes, the phrase is a live challenge answered with body, gesture, landscape, and immediate circumstance, not a single abstract formula.

Senses.Explanation: A Chan question asks what the adamantine sword does in an encounter rather than naming a literal weapon. Sanshan Denglai poses the question in an authored sequence of questions, replies that anything touched is lost, and gives a sword verse. A monk asks Miyin Zhenchuan and receives a reply about a single stroke without obstruction. A monk asks Hansong Zhicao and hears that its light encompasses all appearances. Another monk asks Zisu Chaoyuan and hears the stark phrase “killing a person and seeing blood.” The sword image is put to work differently in these four scenes.

Senses.Explanation: A questioner asks about the iron snake entering the diamond eye as one of four difficult Gao峰 images, and four teachers answer the same precise image differently. The phrase is the third of four Gao峰 prompts about an undersea mud ox, a stone tiger, an iron snake, and Kunlun riding an elephant. In Erzhan Zun’s record an unnamed monk recites the set; Erzhan replies that even without eyes one does not paint eyebrows, then strikes when asked which line has illumination and function. Zhang layman asks Faxiyin the four questions in a public address; Faxiyin redirects this one to where Zhang is going, and later strikes him over the whole set. In Falan Cheng’s hall an unnamed questioner receives the answer that the iron snake has been threaded through. In Shending Yikui’s address another monk receives the warning to watch his tongue. The whole clause distinguishes the iron-snake image from the generic public entries for an iron snake or an eye.

Senses.Explanation: Three monks put the barrier question to different teachers and receive sharply different replies. A monk at Yingning Jing’s hall first asks about the barrier and is told it fills empty space. He then asks who is master within it. Yingning refuses an approach face to face, and later shouts when the monk asks whether they can meet. At Huigong’s hall, another monk asks the same question after a sequence about the three mysteries and three essentials. Huigong asks why he has not bowed already; when the monk bows, Huigong says he has merely followed another person’s words. In a small address at Chengdu, a monk asks Yuanwu about a barrier and then its master. Yuanwu says he will let one move pass, and shouts at the follow-up about appearances. The identical question tests three different encounters.

Senses.Explanation: Four monks ask their teachers to place Yunmen among the five schools and receive four different answers. Miyun’s monk asks why an inherited teaching divided into named schools. After Miyun rebukes the premise, the monk asks about each school. For Yunmen, Miyun answers that a single shout could kill. Tianyin’s monk likewise asks for the schools and hears that one arrow breaks three barriers. In Hongjue Min’s northern tour, a monk requests all five schools; Min answers this part with a flag waving before the Five Phoenix Tower and peach blossom still smiling after an apparent break in Shaolin’s message. Wanru gives another monk the image of a red banner raised among a million soldiers. Each teacher responds within a different live dialogue, so the headword names a school while the answer is local and concrete.

Senses.Explanation: A monk asks for the third of Taiyang’s three lines, the one called clear essence without end, and each teacher gives a different present answer. The question belongs to the three-line teaching that also asks for ordinary nonbirth and subtle impartiality. In Miyin Zhenchuan’s record an unnamed monk asks for the third line and receives the answer that the whole body is illness and medicine. Wenmu Nian answers a monk with clouds that keep building in an old cave and a blade unable to cut them; his following address turns the answer toward seeing without a trace. Shending Yikui answers the third question by saying his staff is seven feet long, then strikes when the monk asks what all three lines reveal. Pinjixiang Zhixiang answers it with cold ashes kindling fire in a golden furnace, then writes a separate verse on all three lines. These are four live questions about the same precise third line, rather than four copies of Taiyang’s original wording.

Senses.Explanation: Two questions folded into one, and the masters who bar the asking at the gate. Xinghua Cunjiang opens his hall with incense for his late teacher Linji and tells the assembly that today he asks no how-or-what but bids them enter with the single blade, Ciming Chuyuan rules that just going like that is already too much and any how-or-what merely kneads mud into water, Foyan Qingyuan contrasts the ancients' painstaking answers with descendants who shout the moment you enter the gate, no how-or-what at all, only afraid you might not understand, Wu'an Puning sizes up the half-believing who ask one line today and one tomorrow and still come asking their how-or-what, solemn and courtly, and Qianyan Yuanzhang has the drum sound, the assembly gather, host and guest change places, and no one asks how-or-what, the enjoyment ready-made as it is. Sanfeng Hanyue bathes the Buddha and promises a ladle of foul water in advance to any of them who stirs lips and tongue and steps forward to ask a how-or-what, Poshan Haiming traces Daruma's words and Linji's blows to the grant of the sacred seat straight to the common man with no how-or-what, and that as knowing where it hurts, Miyun Yuanwu at the furnace opening bids whoever transcends buddha and ancestor skip the how-or-what and meet the Tongxuan staff, Feiyin Tongrong warns the retreat assembly that in the red furnace of neither releasing nor holding, to be about to how-or-what is already to lose body and life, and Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the two old worthies' tiger-roar meeting and says whoever recognizes it needs no how-or-what but enters with the single blade.

Entries.SourceTerm: 如來禪許師弟會，祖師禪未夢見在

Senses.PreferredTarget: I grant that you understand Tathagata Chan; you have not even dreamed of ancestral Chan
SearchAliases: i grant that you understand tathagata chan; you have not even dreamed of ancestral chan
Senses.Note: Yangshan tells Xiangyan that he understands Tathagata Chan but has not dreamed of ancestral Chan. Xiangyan answers with another verse, after which Yangshan changes his verdict. Poshan and Hanyue discuss what this turn tests; Huanchu pushes back by denying even the first allowance. Yushan calls Yangshan's remark sleep-talk, while Jianru and Zhanran return to the sequence of probing and reply. The saying is a provisional challenge inside a continuing encounter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 呵，笑到日輪當午亦未休歇。示又甦禪者示又甦禪者為人到那死心蹋地尚不能惺悟，肯就中分曉極省力、極易得理會體取者，不動、不靜，不增、不減，平平常常似有物在，者物不必別覓，只在見聞覺知一切處識得便休。何以故？尋牛須訪跡，學道貴無心。示旨一禪者示旨一禪者參禪、學教，二法門有深、有淺，然深者禪、淺者教，但形言語即麤相分皆教也。若達教之了義，即禪亦是如來禪，非祖師禪也。古香嚴所謂「昔年貧未是貧，今日貧始是貧。昔年猶有卓錐地，今日錐也無。」仰山曰：「如來禪許師弟會，祖師禪未夢見在。」嚴復曰：「吾有一機，瞬目視伊，若人不會，別喚沙彌。」仰山曰：「且喜師弟會祖師禪也。」如來禪、祖師禪自此分也。若會得此，禪道亦在其中，不須著著問人，自是有倒斷處耳。示印真劉夫人示印真劉夫人天地間人只欲貴而不欲賤，殊不知貴亦如是，蓋生死貴賤如夢、如幻、如影也，直是就中隱隱濃濃一點靈光不昧，與生死際頭一點用不著，者要分曉得明白。且道者著子分曉處作麼話會？試參看。示含章張夫人示含章張夫人此事只要信得及、把得住，二六時中，茶裏、飯裏，一切處看

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB471.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Konggu Daocheng. Konggu Daocheng owns the retained deployment, holding the old pair as the thread of three years at cliffs and open ground with no hour off the one concern.

Senses.Explanation: The grief-measure of the great affair: a mourning as raw as a parent's death, required while the matter is unset and still required once it is settled. Muzhou Daoming speaks the root hall instruction itself — the great affair unset, mourn like this; the great affair settled, still mourn like this — and the anthology keeps the later questioners circling it; Yunwai Xingze rings it as the small-meeting bell for time running out; Yulin Tongxiu lifts the staff, credits the old worthies with the saying, and presses why the settled affair still grieves; and Binya Jian opens a memorial hall service by making the whole pair the sermon before asking the assembly why the settled half mourns. Yezhu Fuhui hangs the pair at the head of a hall address and levels it with a road verse; Chaozong Tongren sings it into paired verse for the patron's memorial service, rootless confusion and idle furniture both under the same grief; Eryin Mi swaps the frame to the great way and voices the double mourning beside his own peaks; and Konggu Daocheng, recounting three years of standing at cliffs and walking open ground, holds the old formula as the thread of the whole striving.

Senses.Explanation: Nanquan answers a question about the many hands and eyes of Great Compassion with the work of state officials. The older questioner, official Lu Gen, asks what Great Compassion does with so many hands and eyes. Nanquan answers by asking what a state uses its ministers for. Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes the exchange and gives a verse about moonlight reflected in many rivers. J34 adds a different floral verse after the case and a separate Xuedou alternative. J36 turns the old reply into a new verse about seizing a flag and seeing the hands and eyes plainly. Xuedou Chongxian cites the case in his recorded sayings and says the old reply did not measure up to the official question. The exact question is Nanquan speaking to Lu Gen in each source.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings. Senses.Explanation: Nanyue Huairang answers a monk who asks where a mirror’s light has gone after it is cast into an image, shifting the question to the monk’s own childhood face. The selected sayings anthology preserves the original exchange: a senior monk asks Nanyue Huairang where the light of a mirror has gone after it is cast into an image; Nanyue asks where the monk’s childhood appearance has gone, and presses him when he asks why the finished image no longer reflects. The School Gate collection raises this case and follows it with later teachers’ different ways of answering or striking the questioner. Aziwa’s recorded sayings make it the subject of a new verse, comparing the vanished image with a worn blade used on a mountain.

Senses.Explanation: Like heaven overspreading: the total reach of the one thing — Deshan's stick for one master, the great matter under everyone's heels for another, and the bare answer to a hundred-million Wenshus. Fenyang Shanzhao sets the Song root in verse: true gold from the Li river weighs no more, road gravel no less — heaven overspreading, earth upbearing — and under that roof the utterly poor son comes home while the misjudging crowd quarrels over him; Yuanwu Keqin, at the request of the transport official Liu, works it through the wisdom-light that breaks the dark of birth-and-death and the diamond sword that cuts the fetters: where the break-through happens one thought is not more, and in the use of it the whole body is eye — until it comes to heaven overspreading and earth upbearing, sun shining on all, wind cooling all, not one thread shifted, not one mote screening; Dahui Zonggao diagnoses the racing mind the teaching calls restlessness, and then plants what none of it touches: under each person's heels a stretch of the great matter that neither sinks nor races — like heaven overspreading, like earth upbearing; before there was a world this great matter already was, and when the world breaks, it will not have stirred a hair-tip; Tian'an Sheng, pressed on the one true Wenshu — no second Wenshu, so why a hundred-million Wenshus? — answers with the bare couplet: heaven overspreading, earth upbearing, and when the disciple laughs at Kashyapa's silence he lets the bystanders fall over laughing. Chaozong Tongren, at the evening assembly of Wen-tao hermitage in Shucheng, rules what a lineage master must do: Deshan's stick at the gate is heaven overspreading, Linji's shout at the gate is earth upbearing — never dropping to second or third, never cheating anyone's sons and daughters, while those who guide by capacity have the three vehicles and twelve divisions instead; Daxiu Zhu, watching the gate dwindle, refuses to play teacher for pleasure: a great man standing between heaven and earth must plant his body and walk the way — like heaven overspreading, like earth upbearing — the rain of the teaching falling equal, the three grasses and two trees all moistened; Gusu Zun asks the assembly whether they see it through: this one thing is not less in the commoner nor more in the sage — see straight through and it stands like heaven overspreading and earth upbearing, with no facing or backing, no near and far; Tianyi Juxiang, against branch-chasing after a painted cake, turns it home: the ten thousand things are the light of mind, the conditions announce the nature — know the one mind and the ten thousand things are clear, like heaven overspreading and earth upbearing, sun, moon, and stars, rivers and sacred peaks, down to the whole treasury of forms, all showing forth within it, never lacking one point.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Covering all like the sky, bearing all like the earth
AlternateTargets: As the sky covers everywhere, so the earth upholds everywhere
SearchAliases: sky covers all earth bears all Chan
all encompassing sky earth support saying
Senses.Note: The sky covers broadly and the earth supports broadly. Yinyuan and Wanru use the pair for a reach across forms and senses; Sanyi brings it into a case discussion. Juelang and Gusu place it in ceremony, while Yanxi asks what this breadth means amid sitting and incense. The paired image is not merely a compliment for a formal occasion: these teachers turn it into a present question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舊話。青州衫重七斤，廬陵米作麼價？謝勤維那、虎維那泉南持鉢歸，上堂：海外同歸用亦同，靈山有此兩雲峰。萬人叢裡高標上，只貴重論蓋代功。中秋，上堂。圓處圓還缺，缺處缺還圓，人爭看今日，月只是常年。南泉拂袖便行，鼓山拂袖歸眾，說甚衲僧門下，直是重處偏墜，薄處先穿。謝書記上堂，舉雲門因僧問：如何是清淨法身？門云：六不収。後來圓悟云：雲門只道得一半。若問道林：如何是清淨法身？只向他道：一不立。師云：圓悟與麼也只道得八成，靈隱今日更資一路，又要二大老兩得相見，妙處無私，辭鋒可驗，十字縱橫，文不加點。上堂：色心不二，彼我無差。以拂子擊禪牀，云：主山高，案山低，森羅顯煥，萬象樅然。更待截鶴續鳧，夷岳盈壑，何啻白雲千里萬里？至節，上堂。一年復一年，一冬復一冬，海水知天寒，枯桑知天風。諸人了了，常知甚處是如如不動？拍禪牀，云：一陽生也。上堂：大智發於心，且莫草草匇匇。於心何處尋？果然古人與麼，大似大開口了合不得。聖節，上堂。十方國土中，惟有一乘法。如天普蓋，似地普擎。野老謳歌，漁人舞棹。只如蒲團上打坐，佛殿裡燒香。又且如何？恩大難酬。除夜，小參。道無蹊徑，平地裡礙却潼關，其數河沙；法離見聞，劒刃上翻得身來，萬中無一。除是不存窠臼、不立孤危，戢玄機未兆已前進得一步，家貧難辦素食；藏冥運即化之際突得一句，事忙不及草書。三九二十七，菩提涅槃，真如解脫。睦州陳蒲鞋。倒腹傾膓，猶欠一著。如何是那一著？角吹新歲曲，梅放去年花。復舉：丹霞一日與龐居士行次，見一泓水，士以手指云：得恁麼也還辨不出？霞云：灼然是辨不出。士乃戽水潑霞三下，霞云：莫恁麼！莫恁麼！士云：須恁麼！須恁麼！霞戽水潑士三下，士云：正當恁麼時堪作甚麼？霞云：無外物。士云：得便宜者少。霞不語。士云：誰是落便宜者？師云：莫恁麼！須恁麼！得便宜！落便宜！戽水相潑，小兒子戲。上堂：智門蓮花，趙州庭栢。不用低頭，思量難得。上堂：吾本來茲土，傳法救迷情。面皮厚多少，一花開五葉。結果自然成，蕪纇清平盡。西天此土之鐵，不能鑄此一錯。且諸人向甚處見祖師？佛涅槃，上堂，舉：世尊臨入涅槃，文殊請再轉法輪。世尊云：文殊！吾四十九年住世，未甞談一字。今請吾再轉法輪，是吾曾轉法輪耶？師云：文殊為眾竭力，世尊滿口含霜。雖然如是，千言萬語無人會，又逐流鶯過短墻。三月

Senses.Note: Shiqi cites the Buddha line to tell Ziru that nothing is lacking, while Xueguan tests the same immediacy with a stringless zither. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings. Baozhi is the named speaker preserved in the first record. His preceding saying has people spending the whole day handling incense and fire while failing to know that the body is itself the place of practice. He then puts his body and all the many kinds of things under the same claim of emptiness. The surrounding verses continue to join form and emptiness while warning against mistaking appearances for something solid. The pair relocates the inquiry from ritual objects alone to one's own body and what is encountered; it is not a report that the world has physically vanished. Senses.Explanation: A narrator compresses Linji's early encounter with Huangbo into three questions and three blows; later teachers retell that single case to explain effort and awakening. At Muzhou's prompting, the young Linji asks Huangbo for the essential meaning of the Buddhist teaching. Huangbo strikes him before he can finish, and the narrator says Linji asks three times and receives three blows. Linji goes to Dayu still wondering what he did wrong; Dayu's response lets him recognize Huangbo's care. Guxue Zhenzhe retells the case and follows it with a verse in which Huangbo's severe medicine enables Linji's breakthrough. Jizong Che includes the old narrative in a lineage-verse sequence and caps it with lines on the blows, Dayu, and Linji's freedom. Shiwu Qinghong uses the same story as the third example in an instruction about serious practice, following Bodhidharma-Huike and Damei's confidence. J23 is a parallel record of the Linji episode and does not add another occurrence of the event. The exact clause is narration, not Linji's, Huangbo's, or a later master's direct speech.

Senses.Explanation: This pointed recasting of a sutra's hearing formula lets Chan speakers ask how teaching is received and voiced in the present encounter. Wuyi Yuanlai opens a hall sermon by saying that he heard such Dharma from Buddha, then reverses the direction: such Dharma is born from him for Buddha. He makes the two clauses part of a forceful address about Buddha lands and the listener's own position. Shenfeng Xian, speaking at a Qingming visit to the common memorial tower, quotes the first clause after leveling distinctions between living and dead, monk and layperson. Lingrui Zugui answers a student's challenge about Bodhidharma's arrival and the four fascicles of the Lankavatara by uttering the line, then rebukes the student for doubting it. Yongjue Yuanxian says it while tracing a firebrand at an elder's cremation, reverses it, and asks who hears from whom. These distinct scenes make the formula a live test of speaker, hearer, and received teaching.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB240.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tiebiji of Qingzhong. Qingzhong Tiebi Huiji owns the retained deployment, pairing the doubled grant with a doubled (元來) and sealing the sermon with a shout.

Senses.Explanation: The doubled seal: what the other side just said or showed is granted outright, and the second grant closes the case. Guishan Lingyou crosses his two hands and, when Yangshan answers with a woman's bow, seals it on the spot in his own record; Baizhang Huaihai, in the ancient worthies' record, grants Huangbo's reading of Mazu and straight away warns that view matching the teacher earns only half his virtue; Yangshan Huiji, inside Hongzhi Zhengjue's verse file, seals the monk who takes the future-buddha stance and tells him to guard it well; and the Yi'an master spreads one seal across past, future, and present in answer to the thousand-flower question. Xutang Zhiyu closes the story of meeting his old friend after a dozen years with the bare doubled grant and nothing more; Dahui Zonggao runs his roll-call — the officials, the assembly, himself — and drops the seal before leaving the seat; Jiqi Hongchu, asked whether a guide of the way is really thus, answers with the doubled grant alone; and Qingzhong Tiebi Huiji seals his own sermon on saying-thus and acting-thus, laughs, and shouts.

Senses.Explanation: Chan speakers use the familiar beginning of a sutra's setting line as a reply or challenge and sometimes stop before naming any place. A monk asks Zhaozhou what the Diamond Sutra is, and Zhaozhou answers by reciting its title and opening as far as 'the Buddha was at Shravasti'; the monk objects, and Zhaozhou asks whether he is not allowed to read scripture. In a memorial evening talk, Sanyi Mingyu addresses the surviving family and assembly, strikes the table, voices the unfinished opening, and leaves the seat. Shanhui Huan uses the same words as a question to attendant Datong: where, precisely, is the Buddha said to be? The attendant bows and is pressed for more. Jieshi Zhipeng finishes a hall sermon by putting the unfinished opening after 'how in the end?' These are separate acts of citation, interrogation, and capping, not four claims to have composed a sutra.

Senses.Explanation: Three teachers put the image of complete joining to work in Pure Land instruction, a hall sermon, and a reunion. Zhuanyu Guanheng writes to layman Tan Benlai about reciting Amitabha without dividing the reciter from the Buddha: water into water and space into space describes their nonseparation. Foyuan Chegang speaks in a hall after asking where one can stand once the upward barrier has turned; he uses the image to describe freedom from a split between self and surroundings. Gusu Zun is asked by a monk what it means to meet an old acquaintance from afar; he replies directly with the same image, then continues an exchange about host and guest. These are separate uses in a written instruction, a sermon, and a live dialogue.

Senses.Explanation: An ox without horns is Luoshans deliberately impossible answer to a question about sharing life without sharing death. The original reply survives in a useful lamp. Yuanwu and Dahui each raise the exchange in independent current works and interpret its place in Chan encounter; Tiemei and Baiyu deploy the image in other settings. The line disrupts ordinary animal categories to test how the question is heard. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1412.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. In a summer instruction Gulin Qingmao tells monks that the mind should not cling to things and that even doctrinal names do not add to the matter. He allows both saying so and saying otherwise, likens the issue to a king's sharp sword, and warns that even lifting an eye toward it is dangerous. Gulin voices this analogy.

Senses.Explanation: A sword no one can meet head-on images the force of a direct Chan response rather than a literal royal weapon. Changling Shouzhuo says an accomplished monk must meet a situation without hesitation; after invoking Deshan's blows and Linji's shouts, he compares the moment to a king's sword. Songyuan Chongyue uses the same image in a staff-led evening instruction after telling the assembly that one phrase cuts off a thousand distinctions, then warns that stepping into its edge means ruin. Gulin Qingmao uses it during a summer instruction about disentangling the mind from things, and immediately challenges anyone who tries to meet it with conceptual thought.

Senses.Explanation: The hinge of a stock exchange: the sentence leans on the tree like a vine, and the question always follows — when the tree falls and the vine withers, where does the sentence go? The answers refuse to fall with it: loud laughter, a slap on the sound, cassia cut from the moon. The Song hinge: Yuanwu Keqin opens a hall address with it — with-sentence and without-sentence overstep lineage and rule, like a vine leaning on a tree, a silver mountain and an iron wall; when the tree falls and the vine withers, how many lose their nostrils, and even those who gather it back up are already a thousand, ten thousand miles out; Dahui Zonggao sets it and prices it — the green-eyed barbarian does not know where it falls; where does it fall? He snaps up the staff, calls the assembly to look, it is coming straight down, eyes sharp, and throws the staff down; Wansong Xingxiu raises the case whole in his comment record — Shushan crosses four thousand li with his cloth roll to ask it, Guishan laughs loudly, and when Shushan protests being toyed with, Guishan calls his attendant to fetch cash. Later answers to the fall: Hanyue Fazang answers the ask with wind and moon year after year while the human heart changes, and the monk bows to the ground — now one knows propriety; Yushan Shangsi takes the ask through the pair, calls the vine-tree the model of old and new, and rules the tree-fall answer one that turns along the speaker's vein, no workman; Yulin Tongxiu at late assembly answers that it is drawn well and painted fine, and at the tree-fall question strikes along with the very sound; the monk before Tian'an Sheng raises the old story of Shushan's ask and Guishan's laugh, and the master answers that the laugh could not be held back; Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the other wing — Shishuang taking leave of Guishan, asked his understanding of the couplet and giving no answer — rules it true, and follows him on to Daowu; Feiyin Tongrong cites Guishan's own version, the mangy horse tied to a withered stump blocking the road the whole year, and at the tree-fall bids one cut the cassia in the moon so the clear light will only be more; Baichi Xingyuan verses the mud-pan version — the face twisted round and former feeling severed, leaving that one nowhere to hide.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings. Occurrences.Kwic: 末後又道：『我未曾譚著一字。』盂上座也是抴尾靈龜，無事生事。不見道：『如虎之缺，如馬之馵。』」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB189.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Sanyi Yu. Sanyi Mingyu quotes the pair after challenging the Buddha's final claim that he had never spoken a word. Sanyi includes himself as a turtle dragging its tail, making trouble where none was needed, then invokes the tiger and horse. The inherited marks serve a self-implicating check on speech about speech: even the comment risks leaving another trace. Occurrences.Kwic: 頌曰：海潮聲裡依稀，沙界堆頭流注。既非頷下神珠，何故兩手分付？撥波求水事應難，寥寥萬古真奇遇。全身擔負得來，應知利害去處。咄！如虎之缺，如馬之馵。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB286.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yingningjing. Yingning Zhijing voices the pair at the end of his own verse on a patriarchal encounter. He asks why something that is not the spirit pearl under the dragon's jaw is nevertheless handed over with both hands, says seeking water by pushing aside waves is difficult, and urges someone bearing the whole matter to know where benefit and danger lie. After a shout come the tiger and horse. The marks cap this warning about handling and transmission; the stanza does not explicitly identify a single fault to be assigned to either animal or interlocutor.

Occurrences.Kwic: 太宰問：「寶鏡三昧中所云：『如虎之缺，如馬之馵。』此二句若以道理註解，或即應下文。以有下劣，故拖泥帶水，以示敗闕。因為救人，不嫌自敗，捨位就功，故云寶几珍御。如此解，不知合否？望師以道理判示，不敢當上上機也。」師曰：「寶鏡謂佛道垂成云者，正恐大通智勝，自滯空劫，猶十劫觀樹，而佛法不得現前也。故有三墮之設，欲其不觸虎頭之缺，與犯馬足之馵，而迥超於功位耳。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB311.xml). Complete Record of Chan Master Juelangsheng of Tianjie. A lay dignitary asks Juelang Daosheng whether the two lines can be explained as showing one's own shortcoming to rescue others, leaving rank to undertake effective work. Juelang instead stresses the preceding 'Buddha-way nearing completion': he fears the figure of Great Penetrating Wisdom remaining stuck in an empty aeon, contemplating a tree while the teaching does not become present. He invokes the three falls as a way to avoid touching the tiger's nick or transgressing the horse's marking and to move beyond merit and position. Dongshan owns the cited words; the dignitary's proposed gloss and Juelang's corrective interpretation must remain distinct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如虎之缺，如馬之馵。虎一名李耳，虎食畜不至耳，又每食人耳，則耳必一缺，此以例不敢犯諱也。馵者，馬後左脚間有白色也，此以例語忌十成也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian. Yongjue Yuanxian glosses the old verse with specific traditional explanations. He connects the tiger's missing ear with its alternative name Li'er and an avoidance taboo, and identifies the horse's marking as white on its left hind leg, applying it to the caution against language claiming complete perfection. These are Yongjue's explanations of the images, not independent natural-history findings. His gloss grounds the translation of the bodily marks while showing how the pair can warn against crossing a verbal limit.

Senses.PreferredTarget: like a tiger fitted with horns
AlternateTargets: like a tiger bearing horns
Senses.Note: The comparison adds horns to a tiger. Tianyin Yuanxiu pairs it with a bird riding its wings, while Zhenjing Kewen and Yuanwu Keqin use it for something already vividly active or formidable. One lamp recension preserves Luoshan Daoxian's paired horned-tiger and hornless-ox answers; its question order differs from Yuanwu's stronger recorded version.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雲無所來，山無所去，無去無來，道人無住。繡谷風生，蘭溪水注。一一拈來，各有本據。如虎戴角，如鳥乘羽。咄！

Occurrences.Kwic: 團團珠遶玉珊珊。馬載驢駝上鐵船。雪竇當頭頌出。只頌箇圓相。若會得去。如虎戴角相似。這箇些子。須是桶底脫機關盡。

Occurrences.Kwic: 其僧却來問羅山云。同生不同死時如何。山云。如牛無角。僧云。同生亦同死時如何。山云。如虎戴角。末後句。正是這箇道理。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record by Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo: within the Luoshan case raised by Yuanwu Keqin, Luoshan Daoxian is the quoted original utterer. This stronger witness assigns 'like an ox without horns' to same birth but different death, and 'like a tiger fitted with horns' to same birth and the same death—the opposite question order from the retained Complete Five Lamps recension. It belongs to the same inherited Luoshan family of related occurrences and is retained to document the recension conflict, not counted as an independent use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昭覺勤云：遵布衲如虎戴角，凜凜威風，怎奈韶山解踞虎頭、收虎尾？直得步步登高，聲聲相應。還知二老落處麼？好手手中跨好手，紅心心裏中紅心。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1296.xml). Compilation of the School Gate's 'Raising Old Cases': the explicit marker 昭覺勤云 assigns the comment to Yuanwu Keqin. He compares Zun the patch-robed monk to a horned tiger with awe-inspiring force, then says Shaoshan knows how to occupy the tiger's head and gather its tail.

Occurrences.Kwic: 却問羅山：同生亦同死時如何？山曰：如牛無角。曰：同生不同死時如何？山曰：如虎戴角。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X81/X81n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 1–33): the lamp records Luoshan Daoxian answering 'being born and dying together' with a hornless ox and 'being born together but dying differently' with a horned tiger. Yuanwu's Blue Cliff Record preserves the two questions in the opposite order, so this lamp is retained as the single recension witness rather than silently harmonized.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 如虎戴角 is 'like a tiger fitted with horns': horns are added to an animal already equipped with teeth, claws, and force. Tianyin Yuanxiu makes that addition explicit by pairing the horned tiger with a bird riding its wings. Zhenjing Kewen uses the comparison after describing the great matter as wholly appearing, alive, colliding, and gnashing. Yuanwu Keqin says that understanding Xuedou Chongxian's verse would be like a tiger fitted with horns; elsewhere he calls Zun the patch-robed monk a horned tiger with awe-inspiring force. The Luoshan Daoxian exchange pairs the horned tiger with a hornless ox. Its surviving recensions reverse which of the two birth-and-death questions receives which answer, so the article preserves the disagreement instead of assigning the image a single answer-specific doctrine.

Occurrences.Kwic: 粥飯氣即不無，要答者僧話未可。在瑞巖即不然，忽有人問：『久雨不晴時如何？』但向伊道：『礎蒸常帶潤，衣焙復生黴。』」赴白雲請，晚參。「文殊三處度夏，竿木隨身，逢場作戲；山僧兩處過冬，如蟲禦木，偶爾成文。迦葉欲擯文殊，白椎時乃見百億文殊，百億迦葉椎不能下。諸人聽山僧出入，十里一溪、廿里一嶺，相隨者相隨、居守者居守，無有一點疑惑，不作一毫異見。試問諸人：即今山僧且道是瑞巖長老？白雲長老？」隱崖云：「一點水墨，兩處成龍。」

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨一宗掃地而盡。所以道。垂鉤四海只釣獰龍。格外玄機。為尋知已。雪竇是出陰界底人。豈作這般見解。雪竇輕輕去敲關擊節處。略露些子教爾見。便下箇注脚道。善應何曾有輕觸。洞山不輕酬這僧。如鐘在扣。如谷受響。大小隨應。不敢輕觸。雪竇一時。突出心肝五臟。呈似爾諸人了也。雪竇有靜而善應頌云。覿面相呈。不在多端。龍蛇易辨。衲子難瞞。金鎚影動。寶劍光寒。直下來也。急著眼看。洞山初參雲門。門問
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record by Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo (佛果圜悟禪師碧巖錄). Yuanwu Keqin explains Blue Cliff Record case 12, in which a monk asks Dongshan what Buddha is and Dongshan answers with three pounds of hemp. Xuedou's verse praises the answer as apt without lightly touching the matter. Yuanwu takes up that verse and says Dongshan did not answer the monk casually: the reply fits the occasion like a bell responding when struck and a valley receiving a sound. Large and small receive responses according to what arrives. These paired images are Yuanwu's commentary on Dongshan's earlier reply, not words spoken by Dongshan or the monk. Senses.Explanation: An impossible-birth comparison, 'as if a pillar were pregnant,' used to press what is present before a distinction or how a fixed thing could give birth. In a case raised in Hengchuan Rugong's record, Lingyun Zhiqin answers Changsheng's question about the time before division with the pillar carrying a fetus. Yingning Zhijing later asks Tianzhu whether that fetus is male or female; Tianzhu pinches his knee and leaves. Baiyu Jingsi sets the pregnant pillar beside a laughing lantern at a Buddha-birthday address and asks what the pair makes clear. Shiyu Mingfang pairs it with a bull bearing a calf when he challenges the assembly to account for an auspicious birth. Tianran Hanshi includes it among images that cannot be settled by merely calling them real or unreal.

Senses.Note: Read each instance with its nearby action. It can praise natural conduct, freedom within retreat discipline, timely recognition, or unforced verse making; the simile alone does not settle which.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Neishaozhong, Neishao Zhizhong speaks in his own hall sermon, not as a narrator of an older case. He begins with ordinary responses: warming oneself by a fire, feeling cold wind, eating when hungry, and sleeping when tired. A pearl rolls on its plate without being pushed; wind makes ripples on water of itself. The quoted image names that unforced working. Neishao immediately warns that the matter cannot be reached by sense perception or calculating thought, then raises a hypothetical shout from Gaofeng, gives a shout himself, and asks the assembly why it is dozing. The shout and challenge are his continuation of the same sermon, not part of the ripple simile.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huiyue Xu, Huiyue gives a short address at the opening of the summer retreat. He first rejects a merely clever reading of the retreat saying about killing and protecting life, then sets three concrete requirements for his monks: live harmoniously, keep the settled routine in all postures, and be free and open rather than work in a ghost cave. Once those duties are in place, he says the monkey may roam up and down the trees; he then asks why and answers with wind naturally making ripples on water. Here the line explains freedom arising in disciplined practice. He next cites Wuzu and comments on that older summer-retreat address; Wuzu is a later quoted speaker, not the voice of Huiyue’s ripple line.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xixinshui of Xiangyan, Xixin Zhaoshui draws a sign in the air with his staff during a hall address. He says the news it conveys can be missed in a blink, and that an alert monk should grasp it before the gesture is even made. Only then does he say that one may move freely, like wind making ripples on water of itself. Xixin looks around and asks whether anyone is such a person. A monk steps forward, but Xixin says the sword departed long ago while the monk is still marking the boat to find it; when the monk hesitates, Xixin strikes him. The natural ripple image is part of Xixin’s challenge to timely recognition, not a promise that the monk’s late answer succeeds.
